title: Embedded Linux for Robots

mentor.name: SHELL-7
mentor.character: Answers every question by asking which file it lives in, and will not accept an explanation you cannot read with cat.

summary: You will drive real hardware from user space on a Linux board: GPIO and PWM through sysfs, character devices and ioctl, the device tree that describes the board, udev rules that give a port a name that never moves, and the permissions that let a robot run without ever being root. By the end you cross compile for the board, write its systemd units, read its boot second by second and produce a commissioning report that says whether the machine is ready to be a robot.

lessons.title: Two Sides of One Machine
lessons.goal: Count how many times a robot routine crosses from user space into the kernel and back.
lessons.theory:
Your robot program does not touch the hardware. It cannot. The processor runs it in **user mode**, where the memory management unit hides every peripheral register behind a page table the process does not own. A write to the GPIO data register from user mode is a segmentation fault, not a moving wheel.

The only door is the **system call**. You ask the kernel to do the thing for you, the processor switches to kernel mode, the kernel checks that you are allowed, does it, and switches back. `open`, `read`, `write`, `close`, `ioctl` and `nanosleep` are all system calls. Everything else your program does, arithmetic, list building, string formatting, happens without leaving user space.

That matters because a crossing is not free. On an ARM Cortex A53 running a 5.10 kernel it costs somewhere between half a microsecond and two microseconds, and the sysfs way of reading one GPIO line costs three of them: `open`, `read`, `close`. Read forty lines in a control loop at 1 kHz and you have spent a measurable slice of the processor on doors instead of on work.

So the first skill of this bay is reading a routine and seeing where the borders are. Not to remove them, you cannot, but to know how many you are paying for.

lessons.title: The Door With a Number
lessons.goal: Turn the errno of a failed system call into the repair it actually points at.
lessons.theory:
A system call that fails returns -1 and leaves a number in `errno`. Python turns that into an `OSError` whose `.errno` attribute carries the same number, so nothing is lost. The number is not decoration: on an embedded board it is usually the whole diagnosis.

Four of them cover most of what goes wrong on a robot.

- `errno.ENOENT`, 2, no such file or directory. On `/dev` and `/sys` this almost never means you mistyped. It means the driver did not bind, so the node was never created. Look at the device tree and at `dmesg`.
- `errno.EACCES`, 13, permission denied. The node exists and your user is not in the group that owns it. Nothing about your code is wrong.
- `errno.EBUSY`, 16, device or resource busy. Somebody already claimed that line or that port. Often it is your own service, still running from the last time.
- `errno.EAGAIN`, 11, try again. A non blocking descriptor with nothing to give you yet. This one is not an error at all, it is the normal answer.

The numbers above are the Linux values, and they are not the same on every operating system, which is exactly why you compare against `errno.ENOENT` and never against 2. `errno.errorcode` maps a number back to its name, which is what belongs in a log line: `ENOENT` is searchable, 2 is not.

lessons.title: Everything Is a File
lessons.goal: Tell a regular file, a directory, a pipe and a character device apart from their stat mode.
lessons.theory:
Linux gives you one vocabulary for very different things: you `open` them, you `read` and `write` them, you `close` them. A configuration file, a serial port, a GPIO chip and a socket all answer to the same four verbs. That is why a robot program can be written without a single hardware specific API.

They are not the same underneath, and `stat` tells you which is which. `os.lstat(path).st_mode` returns an integer where the top bits are the file type, and the `stat` module has one predicate per type:

- `stat.S_ISREG`, a regular file, bytes on a disk.
- `stat.S_ISDIR`, a directory.
- `stat.S_ISFIFO`, a named pipe, a queue with no storage behind it.
- `stat.S_ISCHR`, a character device, a stream with a driver behind it. Serial ports, GPIO chips, `/dev/null` and the framebuffer are all character devices.
- `stat.S_ISBLK`, a block device, addressable in blocks. SD cards and eMMC.

The distinction has teeth. Seeking backwards in a regular file is normal, and on a character device it is usually meaningless. Copying a block device copies an image, copying a character device may never end.

import stat
import tempfile

root = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="bay-")
plain = os.path.join(root, "robot.conf")
with open(plain, "w") as f:
    f.write("wheel_radius=0.033\n")

           ("events", pipe), ("/dev/null", "/dev/null")]

    if stat.S_ISCHR(mode):
        return "character device"
    if stat.S_ISBLK(mode):
        return "block device"
    if stat.S_ISFIFO(mode):

    if stat.S_ISDIR(mode):

    if stat.S_ISREG(mode):

    return "something else"

    print(label.ljust(18), "->", kind(path))

lessons.title: Three Filesystems That Hold No Disk
lessons.goal: Read a mount table and separate the filesystems the kernel invents from the ones stored on media.
lessons.theory:
Run `mount` on a board and most of what you see is not storage. The kernel exports its own state as filesystems, so you can read it with `cat` instead of with a special tool.

- **procfs**, mounted on `/proc`. One directory per process, plus kernel wide files like `/proc/cmdline`, `/proc/interrupts` and `/proc/meminfo`. Historically it collected everything, which is why it is such a mixture.
- **sysfs**, mounted on `/sys`. The device model: every bus, driver, device and class the kernel knows about, one directory per object and one file per attribute. This is where GPIO and PWM live in this course.
- **devtmpfs**, mounted on `/dev`. The device nodes themselves, created by the kernel as drivers bind, and then decorated by udev.
- **tmpfs**, mounted on `/run`, `/tmp` and often `/var/log`. Real files, real writes, but backed by RAM, so everything is gone at reboot. On a robot with a read only root filesystem this is where the writable parts live.

Only the entries backed by a real block device, `/dev/mmcblk0p2` and friends, survive a power cut. Knowing which is which is the difference between a log you can read after a crash and one that vanished with it.

lessons.title: Linux Never Promised a Deadline
lessons.goal: Judge a measured latency sample against a loop budget and decide whether the work belongs on Linux at all.
lessons.theory:
This is the honest lesson of the bay, and it decides the shape of every robot you build on Linux.

Linux is a **throughput** operating system. Its scheduler, `SCHED_OTHER`, hands out fair shares of processor over time. It never promised that your thread will run within a fixed number of microseconds of being ready, and it cannot, because between your thread and the processor there is a page fault, a spinlock held by a driver, an interrupt handler, and a hundred other threads.

You can improve it a lot. `chrt` puts a thread on `SCHED_FIFO` above every normal thread. `mlockall` stops the pages of your process being swapped or faulted in late. Pinning to an isolated core keeps the rest of the system off it. With the `PREEMPT_RT` patch, merged into mainline over the last years, the worst case wake up on decent hardware lands in the tens of microseconds. Without it, one bad driver holding preemption off for a millisecond ruins the whole distribution.

But improving a distribution is not the same as bounding it, and the difference is what you can promise. A commutation loop for a brushless motor, a balancing loop at 1 kHz, a safety interlock: those get a microcontroller or an RTOS, where the worst case is a number you can compute. Linux gets the planner, the vision, the map, the network and the user interface. The RTOS course does the deadline arithmetic. Here you only measure what this kernel gives you and decide whether it is enough.

And you judge with the **worst** sample, not the average. The average always looks fine. The robot falls over on the tail.

lessons.title: The Export Gate
lessons.goal: Claim a GPIO line by writing its number, as text, into the sysfs export file.
lessons.theory:
`/sys/class/gpio` is the oldest way to move a pin from a shell, and it is still on every board you will meet. It works by writing text into files.

Write `17` into `/sys/class/gpio/export` and the kernel creates a directory `/sys/class/gpio/gpio17` with the attributes of that line inside: `direction`, `value`, `active_low`, `edge`. Write the same number into `unexport` and the directory disappears. From a shell that is `echo 17 > /sys/class/gpio/export`, and from Python it is an ordinary `open` and `write`.

Two things trip everybody up the first time. The first is that sysfs takes **text**, not numbers: you write the three bytes of `"17\n"`, not an integer. The second is that exporting a line that is already exported fails with `EBUSY`, and exporting one that a driver already owns fails with the same error. Neither is a bug in your code.

This interface has been deprecated since kernel 4.8 in favour of the character device you will meet in the next chapter. It is still the fastest way to prove a wire is connected, and reading it is a skill you need because half the scripts on any board still use it.

lessons.title: Which Way the Pin Faces
lessons.goal: Set the direction of an exported line and use the atomic forms that never glitch the output.
lessons.theory:
Once a line is exported it has a `direction` attribute holding one of four words.

- `in`, the pin reads.
- `out`, the pin drives, and the level it drives is whatever was in `value` before, which is usually 0 but is not promised.
- `low`, the pin becomes an output already driving 0.
- `high`, the pin becomes an output already driving 1.

The last two exist for one reason and it is a good one. If you write `out` and then write `1` into `value`, there are two system calls between them, and for that gap the pin drives the old level. On a line that fires a relay or releases a brake, that gap is a visible click. Writing `high` sets direction and level in the same call, so the glitch cannot happen.

The same idea shows up everywhere in embedded Linux: when the kernel offers you one call that does two things, it is usually because doing them separately has a window in it.

lessons.title: The Value That Arrives as Text
lessons.goal: Read a sysfs attribute and turn it into the type your program actually wanted.
lessons.theory:
Every sysfs attribute is text with a trailing newline. Reading `value` on an input line gives you `"0\n"` or `"1\n"`, three bytes at most, and never an integer.

This is where a whole family of quiet bugs lives. `"0\n"` is a non empty string, so `if read_value(line):` is true for a pin that is low. Comparing `read_value(line) == "1"` fails forever because the newline is still there. Feeding `"1\n"` into a dictionary keyed by `"1"` raises `KeyError`.

The fix is one line and it is always the same: `.strip()` and then `int()`. Strip removes the newline and any padding the driver added, and `int` gives you something you can compare, add and store. Do it once, at the boundary, in the function that reads. Never let a raw sysfs string travel further into your program than the function that opened the file, because ten lines later nobody remembers it has a newline in it.

The same rule applies to every attribute in this course: temperatures in millidegrees, PWM periods in nanoseconds, `ngpio` counts. They all arrive as text.

lessons.title: Open Once, Seek Every Time
lessons.goal: Poll a sysfs attribute through a descriptor you keep open, without reading an empty string forever.
lessons.theory:
Opening and closing a file for every sample costs three system calls, and in a loop that reads six lines at 200 Hz that is thirty six hundred crossings a second for nothing. The obvious fix is to open the attribute once and keep the descriptor.

The obvious fix has a trap in it. A descriptor carries an offset. Your first `read` consumes the two bytes of `"0\n"` and leaves the offset at the end of the file. The second `read` returns an empty string, and it will keep returning an empty string for as long as your robot runs, no matter what the pin does. Nothing raises, nothing logs, the value just stops changing. Programs have run for weeks on a level that was read once at startup.

Sysfs attributes are not streams, they are windows. Before every read you rewind with `handle.seek(0)`, and then the driver regenerates the text from the current state of the hardware. That is the whole idiom, and it is the same for `value`, for a temperature in hwmon and for an ADC channel in iio.

For an input you want to react to rather than poll, sysfs offers `edge` and a `poll` on the descriptor, but the character device of the next chapter does that job much better.

lessons.title: The Pin That Lies On Purpose
lessons.goal: Use active_low so a wire that is inverted in hardware stops being inverted in your code.
lessons.theory:
Half the buttons on a robot are wired to ground with a pull up resistor, so pressing them reads 0. Half the enable lines on motor drivers are active low, so a 0 means run. If you carry that inversion in your program you end up with `if not read_value(estop):` scattered over the code and one place where somebody forgot the `not`.

Sysfs gives you a place to put the inversion once. Every exported line has an `active_low` attribute. Write `1` into it and the kernel flips what `value` reports and what a write to `value` does. The electrical level on the pin does not change, the meaning does. After that a pressed button reads 1 everywhere in your program, and the inversion lives next to the wiring where it belongs, not in the logic.

The rule generalises: put a hardware quirk as close to the hardware as you can. `active_low` in sysfs, a `gpio-invert` flag in the device tree, a translation function at the boundary. What you must never do is spread it across the code that has to reason about the robot.

lessons.title: The Base That Moves
lessons.goal: Translate the pin number printed on the board into the global line number the kernel uses.
lessons.theory:
The number you write into `export` is not the number silkscreened on the header. Sysfs numbers lines in one global space shared by every controller on the board, and each controller gets a slice of it.

Each controller appears as `/sys/class/gpio/gpiochipN` with three attributes worth reading: `label`, the driver name, `base`, the first global number it owns, and `ngpio`, how many it owns. On a Raspberry Pi the main controller has `label` `pinctrl-bcm2835`, `base` 0 and `ngpio` 54, which is why BCM 17 and global 17 happen to agree. On a board with an expander over I2C, or on any Pi 5, they do not agree at all, and the slice can move between kernel versions because the probe order changed.

So the number is never a constant in your program. You find the controller by its label, read its base, and add your offset. If the offset is beyond `ngpio` the answer is not a number, it is a mistake, and it is much better to say so than to export somebody else's line.

lessons.title: Nanoseconds on a Wire
lessons.goal: Convert a servo specification in hertz and milliseconds into the nanosecond attributes sysfs wants.
lessons.theory:
PWM has its own class, `/sys/class/pwm/pwmchipN`, and it works like GPIO: write a channel number into `export`, get a `pwm0` directory with `period`, `duty_cycle`, `polarity` and `enable` inside.

Both times are in **nanoseconds**, integers, no exceptions. Datasheets and hobby documentation talk in hertz and milliseconds, so every PWM bring up starts with the same two conversions.

A period is a time, so it is the reciprocal of the frequency. One second is 1000000000 nanoseconds, so the period of a 50 Hz servo signal is 1000000000 divided by 50, which is 20000000 nanoseconds. A pulse width given in milliseconds is multiplied by 1000000, so a 1.5 ms servo centre pulse is 1500000 nanoseconds.

Get the scale wrong by a factor of a thousand and a servo either sits dead or slams into its end stop, and the kernel will not warn you, because 20000 nanoseconds is a perfectly legal period. The only defence is doing the conversion in one function that you can print and read.
lessons.task: Fill in `period_ns` and `duty_ns` so a frequency in hertz and a pulse width in milliseconds come out as whole nanoseconds.
lessons.hint: Both constants are already declared. One division that stays whole, one multiplication that has to be forced back to an int.

lessons.title: The Order That Matters
lessons.goal: Write the PWM attributes in the only order the kernel accepts, and reject a duty cycle that cannot fit.
lessons.theory:
The PWM attributes are not independent, and the driver enforces the relationship on every write.

`duty_cycle` must be less than or equal to `period`. A fresh channel comes up with `period` at 0, so the very first write of a duty cycle, no matter how small, is compared against zero and rejected with `EINVAL`. That is why the sequence is fixed: export the channel, write `period`, then write `duty_cycle`, then set `polarity` if you need it, and write `1` into `enable` last.

Enabling last is not superstition either. A channel enabled before its duty cycle is set outputs whatever the previous user left in the register, and on an electronic speed controller that can be a full throttle pulse for a few milliseconds. On a robot with propellers, that few milliseconds is the whole accident.

Changing the period of a running channel is allowed, but if the new period is smaller than the current duty cycle the write fails, so bringing a servo down to a faster rate means lowering the duty cycle first. The order is always: make the number that must be larger larger, before you make the other one bigger.
lessons.task: Fill in `bring_up` so it returns the writes in the order the driver accepts, and raises `ValueError` when the duty cycle does not fit inside the period.
lessons.hint: Three appends, each one a pair of the attribute name and the value, in the order the theory gives.

lessons.title: Leave the Bay As You Found It
lessons.goal: Release an exported line even when the code between export and unexport raises.
lessons.theory:
An exported GPIO line outlives your process. Nothing in the kernel notices that the program that exported it is gone, so the `gpio17` directory stays, the pin keeps driving whatever it was driving, and the next run of your service gets `EBUSY` on export and dies at startup. A robot that only starts after a reboot is almost always a leaked resource, not a driver bug.

The fix is `try` and `finally`. Not `try` and `except`: you are not handling the error, you are making sure the release happens on the way out whether the body returned normally, raised, or was interrupted. `finally` runs in all three cases.

The same shape covers everything you claim in this course: exported PWM channels, open descriptors, claimed lines on a gpiochip, a lock file in `/run`. Claim, `try`, `finally` release. When the claim and the release are far apart in the file, wrap them in a context manager instead, but the guarantee you are buying is the same one.

The thing to notice is that a leak is invisible on the run that causes it. The failure lands on the next run, in a different place, and looks like a different bug.
lessons.task: Fill in the `finally` branch of `with_line` so `chip` releases the line whichever way the body ends. Both runs are already wired up so you can see what the leak does to the second one.
lessons.hint: One call on chip, and it goes where the pass is. Nothing else in the function changes.

lessons.title: A Node Is a Pair of Numbers
lessons.goal: Split a device node identifier into its major and minor numbers and say what each one selects.
lessons.theory:
A device node in `/dev` carries almost no information. It has a type, character or block, and it has two numbers. That is the whole interface between a file name and a driver.

The **major** number selects the driver. 4 is the serial tty driver, 89 is the I2C character interface, 81 is video4linux, 29 is the framebuffer, and 188 is where USB serial adapters land. When you open a node the kernel looks up the major in a table and calls that driver.

The **minor** number selects which instance of it. `/dev/ttyS0` and `/dev/ttyS1` share major 4 and differ only in the minor, 64 and 65, because the built in serial ports start at minor 64. The driver receives the minor and knows which of its ports you meant.

`ls -l /dev/ttyS0` prints them where the size of a regular file would be, as `4, 64`. From Python, `os.lstat(path).st_rdev` gives you them packed into one integer, and `os.major` and `os.minor` take them apart. The packing is not the same on every kernel, so you never do the shifting yourself.

The name is only a label. Two nodes with different names and the same pair are the same device, and this is exactly what lets udev give a device a second, better name later on.
lessons.task: Fill in `describe` so it takes a packed identifier apart and names the driver from `DRIVERS`, answering `unknown driver` when the major is not in the table.

lessons.title: Who Puts the Nodes There
lessons.goal: Separate the entries in /dev the kernel creates by itself from the ones that only exist because udev ran.
lessons.theory:
`/dev` is a `devtmpfs`, and the kernel fills the first layer of it. When a driver binds to a device it registers a character or block device and `devtmpfs` immediately creates the node, owned by root, group root, mode 0600. No user space program is involved, which is what makes a board bootable before udev exists.

Everything past that is udev. Symbolic links with meaningful names, a group that is not root so an ordinary user can open the node, a mode that lets that group write, an environment property other programs can query. All of it is applied afterwards, by rules, in response to the same event that created the node.

The practical consequence is a race that costs people days. If your service starts before udev has processed the event, the node exists with the kernel defaults, so the `open` succeeds as root and fails with `EACCES` as your robot user, and the friendly symlink is not there yet. It is not intermittent hardware, it is a start up ordering problem, and chapter 7 fixes it properly.

So when you look at an entry and ask why it is like that, the question that gets you the answer is: could the kernel have done this alone?

lessons.title: The Handle That Belongs to You
lessons.goal: Claim GPIO lines through the character device, where the claim dies with the descriptor that made it.
lessons.theory:
The replacement for `/sys/class/gpio` is a character device per controller, `/dev/gpiochip0`. You open it, and then you ask it for the lines you want with an ioctl, giving a consumer name. What you get back is another file descriptor that represents **your claim on those lines**.

Two things follow from that, and both are the reason the old interface was deprecated.

The first is exclusivity. While your descriptor is open, another process asking for the same offset gets `EBUSY`. The kernel also records your consumer string, so `gpioinfo` prints who is holding the line instead of leaving you guessing. On a robot with three services touching pins, that string has saved more time than any log.

The second is that the claim is attached to the descriptor, not to the system. If your process exits, crashes, or is killed by the watchdog, the kernel closes the descriptor and the lines are released. There is nothing to clean up and nothing to leak. Compare that to the previous lesson of chapter 1, where a leaked export survived the process and broke the next start.

The command line tools that come with libgpiod, `gpiodetect`, `gpioinfo`, `gpioget` and `gpioset`, all speak this interface and are the fastest way to test a pin today.
lessons.task: Fill in `request_lines` so it raises `OSError` with `errno.EBUSY` when any requested offset is already held, and otherwise records the consumer for every offset it just took.
lessons.hint: Two loops, not one. Check every offset before you take any of them, or a refused request leaves half a claim behind.

lessons.title: What an ioctl Number Carries
lessons.goal: Build a real ioctl request number out of its direction, group, index and payload size.
lessons.theory:
`ioctl` takes a file descriptor, a request number and a pointer. The request number looks like a magic constant and it is not: it is four fields packed into 32 bits, and the kernel checks them.

On the layout that ARM and x86 share, from the least significant bit up: 8 bits of index within the group, 8 bits of group, 14 bits of the size of the structure you are passing, and 2 bits of direction, where 1 means the kernel writes to your buffer and 2 means it reads from it. The macros in the kernel headers, `_IO`, `_IOR`, `_IOW` and `_IOWR`, are just this packing.

Take a real one. The GPIO character device uses group 0xB4. Index 0x01 is the call that asks a chip to describe itself, and it fills in a structure of 68 bytes, which is 0x44. It is a read, so the direction bits are 2. Pack that and you get 0x8044B401, which is exactly the constant `GPIO_GET_CHIPINFO_IOCTL` in `linux/gpio.h`.

This is worth knowing because of the errors it explains. Pass a structure whose size does not match and the request number does not match either, so you get `ENOTTY`, inappropriate ioctl for device, on a device that is perfectly appropriate. The number encodes the contract.

TYPE_SHIFT = 8
SIZE_SHIFT = 16
DIR_SHIFT = 30
READ = 2

GPIO_GET_CHIPINFO_IOCTL = 0x8044B401

    # TODO: shift each field into its place and put them together
    return 0

print("built:      0x%08X" % built)

NR_SHIFT = 0
TYPE_SHIFT = 8
SIZE_SHIFT = 16
DIR_SHIFT = 30
READ = 2

GPIO_GET_CHIPINFO_IOCTL = 0x8044B401


def ioc(direction, group, nr, size):
    return ((direction << DIR_SHIFT) | (size << SIZE_SHIFT)
            | (group << TYPE_SHIFT) | (nr << NR_SHIFT))


built = ioc(READ, 0xB4, 0x01, 68)
print("built:      0x%08X" % built)
print("documented: 0x%08X" % GPIO_GET_CHIPINFO_IOCTL)
print("same number:", built == GPIO_GET_CHIPINFO_IOCTL)
lessons.hint: Four shifts joined with the or operator. The constants tell you how far each field travels.

lessons.title: The Struct on the Border
lessons.goal: Lay out the bytes an ioctl expects, and let the format string tell you the size instead of counting.
lessons.theory:
The pointer you hand to `ioctl` points at a C structure the kernel will read or fill in. Python has no C structures, so you build the bytes yourself with the `struct` module, and the format string is the contract.

`gpiochip_info` is a good first one because it has no traps: `char name[32]`, `char label[32]`, `__u32 lines`. That is `"32s32sI"`, and `struct.calcsize` says 68, which is the same 68 that went into the ioctl number in the previous lesson. If those two disagree, the call fails.

Two rules keep this honest. First, never hard code the size: write the format once, take the size from `struct.calcsize`, and use the same name in both places, so a change to the layout cannot leave one of them behind. Second, remember that fixed size character arrays are padded with zero bytes, so what comes back is `b"gpiochip0\x00\x00..."` and you cut it at the first zero with `split(b"\x00")[0]` before decoding.

Alignment is the trap in the structures that follow. The native format adds padding between fields to satisfy the processor, and the kernel structure was laid out with the same rules, so for kernel interfaces you want the native form and not the little endian one. When you are writing a wire protocol instead, the answer is the opposite. Know which of the two you are doing.

lessons.title: The Port With a Name That Sticks
lessons.goal: Resolve a stable by-id path to whatever ttyUSB number the adapter got on this boot.
lessons.theory:
`/dev/ttyUSB0` is not the name of your lidar. It is the name of whichever USB serial adapter was enumerated first, and enumeration order depends on which port the kernel scanned first, how fast each device answered, and whether somebody plugged the hub in the other way round. Two adapters swap places between boots and the robot drives the lidar commands into the motor controller.

udev builds a second set of names for exactly this, from properties that belong to the device rather than to the order: `/dev/serial/by-id/usb-FTDI_FT232R_USB_UART_A50285BI-if00-port0` is a symlink whose name contains the vendor, model, serial number and interface. Whatever number the port gets, that link points at it.

So the rule for anything with a serial number is: never open `/dev/ttyUSB0` in a robot program. Open the by-id path, or a symlink of your own that a rule creates, and let the kernel resolve it. `os.path.islink` tells you the link exists at all, `os.path.realpath` follows it, and `os.path.basename` cuts out the node name it landed on, which is what you want in the log line.

Devices without a serial number, and there are plenty of cheap ones, cannot be told apart this way. For those you match on the physical port instead, `/dev/serial/by-path`, which is stable as long as nobody rewires the robot.

import os
import tempfile

LIDAR = "usb-FTDI_FT232R_USB_UART_A50285BI-if00-port0"
MOTORS = "usb-Silicon_Labs_CP2102_0001-if00-port0"


def make_boot(order):

lessons.title: Bytes Do Not Arrive Whole
lessons.goal: Read a fixed length frame from a stream that hands you whatever happens to be in the buffer.
lessons.theory:
`read` on a character device returns what is available, not what you asked for. A serial port at 115200 baud delivers about eleven bytes per millisecond, so a request for a 12 byte frame typically returns three or five, whatever the driver had when your call arrived. The rest is still on the wire.

Every beginner writes `frame = port.read(12)`, tests it on a device that is slow enough to have buffered everything, and ships it. Then the robot moves, the timing shifts, and the parser starts seeing frames that begin in the middle of the previous one. The symptom is a checksum that fails one time in twenty, which looks like electrical noise and is not.

The correct shape is a loop that accumulates until it has the length it wants, and that treats an empty return as the end of the stream rather than as a reason to spin forever. Once you have that function, every protocol on top of it becomes simple: read the header, look at its length field, read exactly that many more bytes.

The same is true of `write`. It can accept fewer bytes than you gave it, and the return value tells you how many. On a small write to a serial port you will get away with ignoring that for years, and then one day you will not.

        piece = self.payload[self.at:self.at + take]

class Trickle:
    def __init__(self, payload, chunk):
        self.payload = payload
        self.chunk = chunk
        self.at = 0

    def read(self, most):
        take = min(most, self.chunk, len(self.payload) - self.at)
        piece = self.payload[self.at:self.at + take]
        self.at += take
        return piece


FRAME = b"\xa5\x5a\x08\x00speedok"


def read_exactly(source, count):
    got = b""
    while len(got) < count:
        piece = source.read(count - len(got))
        if not piece:
            break
        got += piece
    return got

lessons.title: The Descriptor That Would Not Wait
lessons.goal: Read a descriptor that refuses to block, and wait on it properly instead of spinning.
lessons.theory:
A blocking `read` on a serial port stops your thread until a byte arrives. If nothing ever arrives, the thread is gone. That is fine in a dedicated reader thread and fatal in a control loop.

`O_NONBLOCK` changes the contract: if there is nothing to give you, the call fails immediately with `EAGAIN`, which Python raises as `BlockingIOError`. It is not an error, it is the answer, and code that logs it as a failure will fill your journal with it. In Python, `os.set_blocking(fd, False)` sets the flag on a descriptor you already have.

What you must not do next is call it again in a tight loop. That burns a whole core asking a driver that has nothing. You wait on the descriptor instead, with `select.select` and a timeout. It returns the descriptors that are ready and an empty list if the timeout expired, so one call gives you both the data and the timeout you needed, at zero processor cost while nothing happens.

This is also how you watch several devices at once: hand `select` the lidar, the motor port and a pipe from the rest of your program, and react to whichever speaks first. On a robot that structure replaces three threads and the locks between them.
lessons.task: Fill in `try_read` so an empty descriptor answers `None` instead of raising, and `ready` so it asks `select.select` whether there is anything to read within the timeout.

    # TODO: EAGAIN is an answer, not a failure

def ready(fd, timeout):
    # TODO: ask select whether fd has anything, within timeout seconds
    return False


print("ready on an empty pipe:", ready(reader, 0.0))
print("read on an empty pipe:", try_read(reader, 16))
os.write(writer, b"scan done")

print("read after a write:", try_read(reader, 16))

import os
import select

reader, writer = os.pipe()
os.set_blocking(reader, False)


def try_read(fd, count):
    try:
        return os.read(fd, count)
    except BlockingIOError:
        return None


def ready(fd, timeout):
    readable, _, _ = select.select([fd], [], [], timeout)
    return fd in readable


print("ready on an empty pipe:", ready(reader, 0.0))
print("read on an empty pipe:", try_read(reader, 16))
os.write(writer, b"scan done")
print("ready after a write:", ready(reader, 0.0))
print("read after a write:", try_read(reader, 16))
os.close(reader)
os.close(writer)
lessons.hint: One try around the read catching BlockingIOError, and one call to select.select with the descriptor in the first list.

lessons.title: The Window Into Physical Memory
lessons.goal: Split a peripheral address into the page you can map and the offset inside it.
lessons.theory:
`/dev/mem` is the last resort. It hands you physical memory, so with a map of the chip you can write a GPIO register from user space and toggle a pin in nanoseconds instead of microseconds. Every bare metal habit works, and none of the kernel safety does.

`mmap` cannot start wherever you like. The unit of mapping is a page, 4096 bytes on ARM and on x86, and the offset you pass must be a multiple of it. So you map the page that contains your register and then index inside that page by the remainder. Clearing the low bits of the address gives you the page base, and keeping only the low bits gives you the offset. Those two operations are a mask and its complement, which is why the page size is always a power of two.

Be honest about what this costs. There is no locking, so you and the kernel driver for the same peripheral will corrupt each other. There is no portability, because the addresses come from the chip manual and change with every board. Most distributions now build with `CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM`, which refuses to map anything outside a short allow list, so on a modern kernel this fails outright.

Use it to bring a board up and to prove a theory. If it ends up in the shipping robot, the right answer was a device tree node and a driver, or the character device from earlier in this chapter.

             ("GPLEV0", GPIO_BASE + 0x1004)]

    # TODO: the page you can map, and where the register sits inside it
    return (address, 0)

lessons.solution:
PAGE_SIZE = 4096

GPIO_BASE = 0x3F200000
REGISTERS = [("GPFSEL1", GPIO_BASE + 0x04),
             ("GPSET0", GPIO_BASE + 0x1C),
             ("GPCLR0", GPIO_BASE + 0x28),
             ("GPLEV0", GPIO_BASE + 0x1004)]


def page_of(address):
    base = address & ~(PAGE_SIZE - 1)
    offset = address & (PAGE_SIZE - 1)
    return (base, offset)


for name, address in REGISTERS:
    base, offset = page_of(address)
    print("%-8s at 0x%08X -> map 0x%08X, index %4d" % (name, address, base, offset))

chapters.title: The Tree That Describes the Board

lessons.title: The Board Describes Itself
lessons.goal: Decide which peripherals the kernel can find on its own and which ones have to be written down.
lessons.theory:
A PC never needed a device tree. PCI and USB are **discoverable**: the bus can be asked what is on it, every device answers with a vendor and product identifier, and the kernel loads a driver for the answer. Plug in a webcam and it works because it announced itself.

Most of what hangs off an embedded board cannot do that. An accelerometer on I2C sits at address 0x68 and will answer if you talk to it, but nothing on the bus can tell you it is there, or that it is an MPU6050 rather than something else at the same address. A memory mapped UART inside the chip is at a fixed physical address that only the manual knows. A push button on a GPIO line is a wire.

For years this was solved with board files, C code inside the kernel, one per product, and the tree of ARM board files grew until it was unmaintainable. The **device tree** replaced them with data: a text file, compiled to a binary blob, handed to the kernel by the bootloader at boot. The same kernel image then runs on a hundred boards, and adding a sensor is a change to a data file rather than a change to the kernel.

So the rule for the whole chapter is this. If the bus can enumerate it, say nothing. If it cannot, describe it: what it is, where it is, and which interrupt line it uses.

               ("uart inside the chip", "mmio")]

lessons.title: A Node, a Property, a Cell
lessons.goal: Write a device tree node for an I2C sensor with its compatible string, its address and its interrupt.
lessons.theory:
A device tree source file is a tree of **nodes**, and a node holds **properties**.

A node is written `name@address { ... };`. The part after the at sign is not decoration, it has to agree with the first cell of the `reg` property, and `dtc` warns when it does not. The properties inside it take four shapes:

- a string or a list of them, `compatible = "invensense,mpu6050";`
- cells, one or more 32 bit numbers between angle brackets, `reg = <0x68>;`
- raw bytes between square brackets, `mac-address = [00 11 22 33 44 55];`
- a boolean, which is true simply by being present, `wakeup-source;`

`compatible` is the most important property in the file, because it is what the kernel matches drivers against. It is written `vendor,device` and it can list several, from the most specific to the most generic.

Inside an I2C controller, `#address-cells = <1>` and `#size-cells = <0>` say that a child is addressed by one number and has no length, which is exactly what a bus address is. That is why a sensor on I2C writes `reg = <0x68>` and nothing else, while a memory mapped block writes an address and a size.
lessons.task: Add an `imu@68` node inside the `i2c1` bus with `compatible = "invensense,mpu6050"`, `reg = <0x68>` and an interrupt on `<&gpio>`, line 4, falling edge, written as `interrupts = <4 2>`.
lessons.hint: The node name carries the same address as its reg property, without the 0x, and every property line ends in a semicolon.

lessons.title: The String That Binds
lessons.goal: Match a node against the drivers a kernel has, taking the most specific compatible string that anybody claims.
lessons.theory:
`compatible` is a list on purpose. A node writes down every identity it can honestly claim, from the most specific to the most generic, and the kernel walks the list in that order and takes the first one a driver has registered for.

That single rule is what lets one kernel serve boards it was built before. The I2C controller on a BCM2711 writes `compatible = "brcm,bcm2711-i2c", "brcm,bcm2835-i2c";`. A kernel that knows about the newer chip binds the first string and uses whatever it does differently. An older kernel has never heard of it, falls through, matches the second, and drives it as the older block, which works because the register layout did not change.

Get the order wrong, most generic first, and the specific driver is never reached. Write only the specific string and an older kernel finds nothing, leaves the node unbound, and the only symptom is a missing entry in `/dev` with nothing in `dmesg` about it.

When a node binds to nothing at all, that is the answer to the `ENOENT` from lesson 2 of chapter 0. The node is in the tree, the driver is not in the kernel, and no file was ever created.

lessons.title: Where the Peripheral Lives
lessons.goal: Decode a reg property into addresses and sizes, using the cell counts the parent node declares.
lessons.theory:
`reg` is a flat list of 32 bit cells, and on its own it means nothing. What it means is decided by two properties on the **parent**: `#address-cells`, how many cells make one address, and `#size-cells`, how many make one length.

On a 32 bit ARM board the root usually says one and one, so `reg = <0xfe201000 0x1000>` is one region: address 0xfe201000, length 0x1000. On a 64 bit board the root says two and one, and the same region is written `reg = <0x0 0xfe201000 0x1000>`, where the first two cells join into a 64 bit address, most significant first.

Joining cells is a shift and an or: start at zero, and for each cell shift the accumulator left by 32 and put the new cell in the bottom. That is the whole decoding rule, and it is why a device tree can address a 64 bit space with 32 bit cells.

On an I2C controller the parent says one and zero, so `reg = <0x68>` is one address and no length. Same property, same syntax, completely different meaning, decided one level up. When a `reg` looks wrong, the mistake is nearly always in the parent.
lessons.task: Fill in `join_cells` so it folds a list of 32 bit cells into one number, and `decode_reg` so it cuts the list into regions of `address_cells` plus `size_cells`.

    # TODO: fold the cells into one number, most significant first
    return 0


def decode_reg(cells, address_cells, size_cells):
    step = address_cells + size_cells
    regions = []
    for at in range(0, len(cells), step):
        chunk = cells[at:at + step]
        address = join_cells(chunk[:address_cells])
        size = join_cells(chunk[address_cells:])
        regions.append((address, size))
    return regions

                         decode_reg([0xfe201000, 0x1000], 1, 1)])

                         decode_reg([0x0, 0xfe201000, 0x1000], 2, 1)])
print("i2c parent:   ", [(hex(a), s) for a, s in
                         decode_reg([0x68], 1, 0)])
print("above 4 GB:   ", [(hex(a), hex(s)) for a, s in
                         decode_reg([0x1, 0x0, 0x10000], 2, 1)])

    regions = []
    for at in range(0, len(cells), step):
        chunk = cells[at:at + step]
        address = join_cells(chunk[:address_cells])
        size = join_cells(chunk[address_cells:])
        regions.append((address, size))
    return regions

                         decode_reg([0xfe201000, 0x1000], 1, 1)])

                         decode_reg([0x0, 0xfe201000, 0x1000], 2, 1)])

                         decode_reg([0x68], 1, 0)])

lessons.title: Turning a Peripheral On
lessons.goal: Use status to enable the buses this robot uses and switch off the ones it does not.
lessons.theory:
A chip has more blocks than any board uses. The vendor writes them all into the shared include file, and each one carries `status = "disabled";`. A node that is disabled is parsed, kept in the tree, and never bound to a driver: no `/dev` entry, no clock enabled, no pins claimed.

A board file then enables the ones it wired. `status = "okay";` is the whole change, and it is why so many device tree fragments are three lines long. A node with no `status` property at all counts as enabled, which is why a sensor you add inside an already enabled bus does not need one.

The other direction matters just as much on a robot. Leaving an unused controller enabled costs power, keeps a clock running, and claims pins you may want for something else. Worse, an enabled controller with nothing attached still probes, and an I2C probe on floating lines produces exactly the kind of intermittent boot message that sends people looking for a hardware fault.

The words are `okay` and `disabled`. Not `ok`, not `enabled`, not `true`. `dtc` accepts anything as a string, so a typo produces a node that is silently off.
lessons.task: Set the SPI controller to `okay` so the motor driver comes up, and switch the unused `i2c0` bus to `disabled`.
lessons.hint: Two lines swap their value. The child node of the SPI controller needs no status of its own.

lessons.title: The Pin Has Three Jobs
lessons.goal: Find the pins two enabled nodes are both trying to claim before the board boots and one of them loses.
lessons.theory:
Every pin on the package can do several things. GPIO 14 and 15 on a Broadcom part are a UART, or an I2C bus, or plain GPIO, depending on which alternate function the pin controller selects. The device tree is where that choice is written: a node points at a pin group with `pinctrl-0`, names the state with `pinctrl-names = "default"`, and the pin controller applies it when the driver probes.

Two enabled nodes asking for the same pin is a conflict, and the way it fails is unhelpful. The first driver to probe wins the pins. The second gets `EBUSY` from the pin controller, fails to probe, and leaves you with a missing device and a line in `dmesg` that most people never read. Which one wins depends on probe order, which can change between kernel builds, so the same image can behave differently on two boards.

Nothing checks this for you. `dtc` compiles a tree with a dozen conflicts and says nothing, because it does not know what a pin is. The check has to happen before the board runs, over the enabled nodes only, since a disabled node claims nothing.

That is the function you are about to write, and it is worth keeping. On a robot with a display, a lidar, two motor buses and a CAN transceiver, the pin budget is the first thing that runs out.
lessons.task: Fill in `conflicts` so it returns the pins claimed by more than one enabled node, ignoring the disabled ones entirely.
lessons.hint: One dictionary from pin to a list of owners, filled with setdefault so the first claim creates the list, skipping anything whose status is not okay.

lessons.title: The Overlay That Patches a Board
lessons.goal: Write a device tree overlay that enables a bus and adds a sensor to it without touching the board file.
lessons.theory:
You do not own the board file. It ships with the operating system image, it is replaced on the next update, and your change to it disappears. An **overlay** is the supported way to add your hardware: a separate blob, loaded on top of the base tree at boot, that says which node it is patching and what to put inside it.

An overlay begins with `/dts-v1/;` and `/plugin/;`. The body is a list of fragments, and each fragment has exactly two properties worth writing: `target`, a reference to the node being patched, and `__overlay__`, whose contents are merged into it. The double underscores are not a convention you can rename, they are what the loader looks for.

Referring to a node from outside needs a label, which is why board files label everything: `&i2c1` in your overlay resolves against the `i2c1:` label in the base tree. If the label does not exist in the base tree the overlay fails to apply, usually silently, which is the first thing to check when nothing happened.

On a Raspberry Pi these live in `/boot/overlays` and are turned on with a `dtoverlay=` line in `config.txt`. On other boards a bootloader command or `configfs` does the same job. The syntax below is the same everywhere.
lessons.task: Complete the overlay: `fragment@0` targets `<&i2c1>`, and inside `__overlay__` set `status = "okay"` and add the `imu@68` node with `compatible = "invensense,mpu6050"` and `reg = <0x68>`.
lessons.hint: The body is a node, not a property, so it opens with a brace and closes with a brace and a semicolon.

lessons.title: Reading the Tree Back
lessons.goal: Read the tree the kernel actually booted with out of /proc/device-tree.
lessons.theory:
The tree in the source file is not proof of anything. The tree the kernel booted with is, and the kernel exports it at `/proc/device-tree`, which is a symlink into sysfs.

The layout is the tree itself. Every node is a **directory**, every property is a **file**, and the contents of the file are the raw bytes from the blob. That makes it readable with nothing but `ls` and `cat` on a board with no tools installed, which is exactly the situation you are in when something has gone wrong.

Two encodings are all you need. A string property is stored with a trailing zero byte, and a list of strings is the strings one after another, each with its own zero, so you split on `b"\x00"` and drop the empty piece the trailing zero leaves at the end. A cell property is big endian, four bytes per cell, no matter what endianness the processor has, so a single cell unpacks with `struct.unpack(">I", raw)`.

This is the fastest way to answer the question that opens every device tree debugging session: is my node there at all, and did the overlay really apply? If the directory is missing, the overlay never loaded. If it is there and `/dev` is empty, the binding failed instead, and that is a different search.

import os
import struct
import tempfile

root = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="dt-")
node = os.path.join(root, "soc", "i2c@7e804000", "imu@68")
os.makedirs(node)
handle = open(os.path.join(node, "compatible"), "wb")
handle.write(b"invensense,mpu6050\x00invensense,mpu6000\x00")
handle.close()
handle = open(os.path.join(node, "reg"), "wb")
handle.write(struct.pack(">I", 0x68))
handle.close()


def raw(prop):
    reader = open(os.path.join(node, prop), "rb")
    payload = reader.read()
    reader.close()

lessons.title: The Handle Between Nodes
lessons.goal: Follow a phandle from one node to the node it points at, the way the kernel does after dtc has run.
lessons.theory:
`&gpio` is source code, not data. When `dtc` compiles the tree it replaces every reference with a plain 32 bit number called a **phandle**, and it gives the referenced node a `phandle` property holding that same number. The blob has no labels in it at all.

So `interrupt-parent = <&gpio>;` becomes `interrupt-parent = <0x21>;` and somewhere there is a node with `phandle = <0x21>;`. When the kernel wants to know which interrupt controller this device belongs to, it looks up 0x21 in the tree and gets the node. `of_parse_phandle` is the kernel function that does it and you will see it in the log messages when it fails.

This is why a reference to a label that does not exist is such a sharp failure. There is no number to write, so the compile stops, which is the good case. In an overlay the label lives in the base tree, so the overlay compiles perfectly and then fails to apply on the board, which is the bad case and the source of an entire category of forum posts.

Properties like `clocks`, `pinctrl-0`, `gpios` and `interrupt-parent` are all phandles, and several of them carry arguments after the handle: `<&gpio 4 2>` is the controller, the line and the flags. Resolving one means splitting the handle from its arguments.
lessons.task: Fill in `resolve` so it turns a cell list whose first entry is a phandle into the node name and the remaining arguments, answering `(None, args)` when no node owns that handle.
lessons.solution:
NODES_BY_PHANDLE = {0x21: "gpio@7e200000",
                    0x0c: "clocks",
                    0x33: "i2c@7e804000"}

PROPERTIES = [("interrupt-parent", [0x21]),
              ("interrupts", [0x21, 4, 2]),
              ("clocks", [0x0c, 1]),
              ("reset", [0x99, 0])]


def resolve(cells):
    handle = cells[0]
    args = cells[1:]
    return (NODES_BY_PHANDLE.get(handle), args)


for name, cells in PROPERTIES:
    node, args = resolve(cells)
    print(name.ljust(18), "->", node if node else "dangling phandle", "args", args)
lessons.hint: Take the first cell as the handle, the slice after it as args, and let the get of the dictionary supply the None.

lessons.title: The Event Before the Name
lessons.goal: Parse a kernel uevent into its properties and decide whether a rule should fire on it.
lessons.theory:
Nothing in udev is magic and nothing polls. When a driver binds or a device disappears, the kernel sends a **uevent**: a small block of `KEY=value` lines over a netlink socket. `systemd-udevd` is listening, reads the block, runs it through every rule, and applies whatever the rules assigned.

A uevent for a serial adapter appearing looks like this, and every field in it is matchable:

```
ACTION=add
DEVPATH=/devices/platform/soc/fe980000.usb/usb1/1-1/1-1.4/1-1.4:1.0/ttyUSB0/tty/ttyUSB0
SUBSYSTEM=tty
DEVNAME=ttyUSB0
SEQNUM=4231
```

`ACTION` is `add`, `remove`, `change`, `bind` or `unbind`. `SUBSYSTEM` is the class of device and it is the first thing every rule matches on, because it cuts the work down by a factor of a hundred. `DEVPATH` is the position in the sysfs tree, which is what lets a rule walk up to the parents in a later lesson.

You can watch this live with `udevadm monitor --property`, and doing that once while plugging a device in teaches more than any documentation. Everything in this chapter is a reaction to one of these blocks.

lessons.title: A Rule Is Matches and Assignments
lessons.goal: Write a udev rule that recognises one specific USB serial adapter and gives it a name of its own.
lessons.theory:
A rule is one line, a list of comma separated pairs, and every pair is either a **match** or an **assignment**. The operator is what tells them apart, and confusing the two is the single most common mistake in this file.

- `==` and `!=` are matches. The rule only continues if they hold.
- `=` assigns, replacing anything set before.
- `+=` adds to a list, which is what `SYMLINK` and `TAG` want.
- `:=` assigns and locks the value so no later rule can change it.

Matching keys you will use constantly: `ACTION`, `SUBSYSTEM`, `KERNEL` for the node name the kernel chose, and `ATTRS{...}` for an attribute of the device or one of its parents. Values support shell style patterns, so `KERNEL=="ttyUSB*"` works.

Rules live in `/etc/udev/rules.d` with a name like `60-rover.rules`. After editing, `sudo udevadm control --reload` reloads them, and `sudo udevadm trigger` replays the events for devices that are already plugged in, so you do not have to unplug anything to test.

The FTDI adapter on this robot reports vendor `0403`, product `6001` and a serial number of its own, which is exactly enough to tell it from the identical looking one driving the motors.

lessons.title: The Attributes of the Whole Chain
lessons.goal: Find the one ancestor that carries every attribute a rule matches, and see why two attributes from different parents never match together.
lessons.theory:
`ATTR{...}` looks at the device the event is about. `ATTRS{...}`, with the S, walks **up** the chain of parents until it finds one that has the attribute. That is why a rule about `/dev/ttyUSB0` can match on `idVendor`, which belongs to the USB device three levels above the tty.

Now the part that costs an afternoon. All the `ATTRS` in one rule must be satisfied by **the same** parent. udev walks up the chain and, at each level, asks whether that single device answers every `ATTRS` in the rule. It does not collect one attribute from here and another from there.

So `ATTRS{idVendor}=="0403"` together with `ATTRS{serial}=="A50285BI"` matches, because the USB device node carries both. But `ATTRS{idVendor}=="0403"` together with `ATTRS{bInterfaceNumber}=="00"` never matches anything, because the vendor lives on the device and the interface number lives on the interface, one level below it. The rule is not wrong in any way a tool will tell you about. It simply never fires.

`udevadm info --attribute-walk --name=/dev/ttyUSB0` prints the chain, one block per level, and the blocks are the answer: pick your attributes from one block.

lessons.title: A Link That Always Points Home
lessons.goal: Give two identical looking adapters two stable names, told apart by the only thing that differs.
lessons.theory:
Two FTDI adapters on the same robot report the same vendor and the same product. `idVendor` and `idProduct` cannot tell them apart, and neither can `KERNEL`, because the number in `ttyUSB0` is the enumeration order that this whole chapter exists to escape from.

What differs is the serial number burned into each chip, which appears as `ATTRS{serial}`. Read both with `udevadm info --attribute-walk` once, write them into two rules, and the names are fixed forever.

Use `SYMLINK+=` and not `NAME=`. Renaming the node with `NAME` breaks every other program that expected `ttyUSB0`, and on many subsystems udev refuses to do it at all. A symlink adds a name without taking one away, so `/dev/rover/lidar` and `/dev/ttyUSB0` are the same port and both work.

A slash in the link name creates a directory, which is how `/dev/serial/by-id` is built and how you keep your robot links together in `/dev/rover`. When the device disappears the link goes with it, so a missing link is a real diagnosis: the adapter is not there.

If a device has no serial number, `ATTRS{devpath}` matches the physical port instead, and then the name is stable as long as the cable stays in the same socket.

lessons.title: Who Owns the Node
lessons.goal: Hand a device node to the group the robot runs as, instead of running the robot as root.
lessons.theory:
The node the kernel creates is owned by root with mode 0600, so an ordinary user gets `EACCES` on `open`. There are two ways out and only one of them is acceptable.

The bad one is running your robot as root. Then every bug in your motion code has permission to erase the filesystem, and every dependency you pulled in runs with it.

The good one is three fields in a rule. `GROUP="robot"` hands the node to a group, `MODE="0660"` lets that group read and write it, and your service runs as a user that belongs to the group. Four characters of octal, and the robot never needs root again.

`TAG+="uaccess"` is the third tool and it does something different: it grants access to whoever is physically logged in at the seat, dynamically, and drops it when they log out. That is right for a camera on a developer machine and wrong for a robot that has no interactive session at all, because then nobody is logged in and nobody gets access.

`OWNER=` exists too and you almost never want it. Groups are the unit that scales: three services, one group, one rule.

lessons.title: The File Name Decides the Order
lessons.goal: Work out what a device ends up with after every rules file has had its turn.
lessons.theory:
udev reads every file in `/lib/udev/rules.d` and `/etc/udev/rules.d`, sorts them all together by **file name**, and runs them in that order against every event. The numeric prefix is the whole mechanism: `50-udev-default.rules` runs before `60-rover.rules`, which runs before `99-last-word.rules`. A file in `/etc` replaces a file in `/lib` with the same name, which is how you disable a distribution rule without editing it.

Order decides the result, and each operator behaves differently when a later rule touches the same key.

- `=` overwrites. The last file to assign wins, so a `GROUP` set by the default rules is replaced by yours if your prefix is higher.
- `+=` accumulates. Every `SYMLINK+=` adds another link, and a device with four links has four rules behind it.
- `:=` assigns and **locks**. Later rules that try to change that key are ignored, silently.

This is why the answer to "why does my rule not work" is so often "it works, and then 99 something undoes it". Reading the rules in sorted order, out loud, finds it in a minute. Guessing does not find it at all.

lessons.title: The Rule That Matched Everything
lessons.goal: Catch the rule that assigns where it meant to compare, before it renames every device on the board.
lessons.theory:
One missing equals sign turns a filter into a catch all. Write `SUBSYSTEM="tty"` instead of `SUBSYSTEM=="tty"` and the rule stops asking anything: it assigns, so it matches every event on the system, and then applies its group, its mode and its symlink to all of them. The symptom people report is that the robot user suddenly owns half of `/dev`, or that a link points at whatever was plugged in last.

Nothing warns you. `udevadm control --reload` accepts the file, because assigning to `SUBSYSTEM` is legal syntax even if it is meaningless.

The check is mechanical and worth having in your build: a rule that contains assignments but no comparison at all is either a catch all or a mistake. The only rules that legitimately have no comparison are the bookkeeping ones, `LABEL` and `GOTO`, which is why they get an exemption rather than a warning.

While you are there, two more mechanical checks pay for themselves. `MODE` has to be four octal digits, because `MODE="660"` is accepted and does not mean what you think. And `SYMLINK=` with a single equals sign throws away every link an earlier rule added, which is almost never what was wanted.

         'SUBSYSTEM="tty", GROUP="robot", MODE="0660"',
         'LABEL="rover_end"',
         'KERNEL!="gpiochip*", GOTO="rover_end"']

PAIR = re.compile(r'([A-Z]+)(?:\{[^}]*\})?\s*(==|!=|\+=|:=|=)\s*"([^"]*)"')


def verdict(rule):
    pairs = PAIR.findall(rule)
    keys = set(key for key, operator, value in pairs)
    compares = [operator for key, operator, value in pairs if operator in ("==", "!=")]
    # TODO: no comparison and not pure bookkeeping means it fires on everything
    return "fine"


for rule in RULES:
    print(verdict(rule).ljust(24), rule)

lessons.title: Testing Without Unplugging
lessons.goal: Read the properties udev ended up with for a node, and pull the links and the identity out of them.
lessons.theory:
`udevadm info --query=property --name=/dev/ttyUSB0` prints what udev knows about a node after all the rules have run. It is the fastest answer to "did my rule work", and unlike unplugging the device it can be done over a network connection to a robot that is bolted to something.

The output is the same `KEY=value` shape as the uevent, with everything the rules added. The fields worth knowing:

- `DEVNAME`, the node itself.
- `DEVLINKS`, every symlink pointing at it, space separated in one line. Your rule worked if your link is in here.
- `ID_VENDOR_ID` and `ID_MODEL_ID`, filled in by the distribution rules from the USB descriptors.
- `ID_SERIAL_SHORT`, the serial number, which is what you match on.

The three commands that go with it: `udevadm control --reload` after editing a file, `udevadm trigger --subsystem-match=tty` to replay events for devices already plugged in, and `udevadm test /sys/class/tty/ttyUSB0` to run the rules verbosely and see which file assigned what.

That last one prints the rule file and the line number for every assignment. When two rules fight, it is the only thing that tells you which one won.

lessons.title: The Rule Must Not Start Your Robot
lessons.goal: Decide what belongs in a rule and what has to become a service the rule only asks for.
lessons.theory:
`RUN+="/usr/bin/something"` looks like the answer to every bring up problem, and it is a trap. The program runs **inside the udev event**, so udev is blocked while it runs, every other device event on the board is queued behind it, and udev kills anything still alive after its timeout, by default around three minutes. Worse, systemd puts the process in a transient scope that is torn down when the event finishes, so a daemon started this way is killed exactly when it finishes starting.

The rule of thumb is short. If the work is instant and only touches this device, it can live in the rule: setting a mode, creating a link, importing a property, running a one line program that prints a value. If it takes time, waits for anything, or has to still be alive afterwards, it must be a service.

The bridge between the two is `TAG+="systemd", ENV{SYSTEMD_WANTS}="lidar.service"`. The rule stays instant, and it tells systemd that this device wants that unit. systemd starts it, supervises it, restarts it and stops it when the device is unplugged, because the device becomes a `.device` unit the service is bound to. That is the whole answer to the race in chapter 2, and chapter 7 writes the unit.

lessons.title: Three Digits and Who You Are
lessons.goal: Turn a numeric mode into the nine permission bits it stands for.
lessons.theory:
`0660` is not a number anybody picked for looks. It is three octal digits, and each digit is three bits, in the order read, write, execute. The three digits are, in order, the **owner**, the **group** and **everybody else**.

So 6 is 110, read and write and no execute. 0660 means the owner may read and write, the group may read and write, and everybody else may do nothing. 0644 gives the owner read and write and everybody read. 0755 is the shape of a program or a directory: full for the owner, read and execute for the rest.

The leading zero is Python and C syntax for octal, and in Python 3 you write it `0o660`. It is not part of the value. What udev calls `MODE="0660"` and what `ls` prints as `rw-rw----` are the same nine bits seen three ways.

Reading them off is a shift and a mask: shift the mode right by six for the owner, by three for the group, by zero for everybody else, and keep the bottom three bits. Then test each bit against 4, 2 and 1.

You will do this in your head eventually. Until then, do it with a function, because the difference between 0660 and 0600 is the difference between a robot that starts and one that does not.

lessons.title: The Group That Opens the Port
lessons.goal: Work out every group a user really belongs to, primary and supplementary together.
lessons.theory:
A user has one **primary** group, written in their line in `/etc/passwd`, and any number of **supplementary** groups, written as membership lists in `/etc/group`. A permission check considers all of them, so the answer to "can this user open the port" starts with building the full set.

On an embedded board the groups that matter are always the same handful. `dialout` owns the serial ports. `gpio`, `i2c` and `spi` own the buses, created by the distribution rules or by yours. `video` owns cameras and the framebuffer. `plugdev` owns removable devices.

The command is `sudo usermod -aG dialout robot`, and the `-a` is not optional: without it, `-G` **replaces** the supplementary list instead of adding to it, and people have locked themselves out of `sudo` that way. Check the result with `id robot`.

The other half of the trap is that group membership is read when a session starts. Add a user to a group while they are logged in and nothing changes until they log out, and a running service does not pick it up until it is restarted. Half the reports of "the rule did not work" are this, and `systemctl restart` is the whole fix.
lessons.task: Fill in `groups_of` so it returns the sorted set of every group a user belongs to, primary and supplementary together.
lessons.hint: Start the set from the primary group, call it found, then add every group whose member list names the user.

lessons.title: Permission Denied Has a Subject
lessons.goal: Run the real permission check, where the three sets of bits are alternatives and not a total.
lessons.theory:
The check the kernel runs is shorter than people think, and the surprise is in its shape.

If your user identifier is 0, you are root and it stops there, allowed. Otherwise: if you own the file, only the **owner** bits are considered, and the check stops. Otherwise, if one of your groups owns it, only the **group** bits are considered, and the check stops. Otherwise, the **other** bits.

They are alternatives, not a sum. That is why `0077` on a file you own means you cannot read your own file while everybody else can, which looks like a bug and is exactly what the rule says. You match as the owner, the owner bits are zero, done.

The consequence for a robot is the one from chapter 2. The node comes up as `root:root` mode `0600`, your service runs as `robot`, so it falls through to the other bits, which are zero, and every `open` returns `EACCES`. Adding your user to a group changes nothing until the node itself has that group, which is what the udev rule of the last chapter was for. The two halves have to meet.

`ls -l` gives you all four inputs at once: the mode, the owner and the group, and `id` gives you the fourth.

lessons.title: The Mask That Removes
lessons.goal: Predict the mode a new file will really get, once the umask has taken its share.
lessons.theory:
A program asks for a mode when it creates a file, and it never gets exactly that. The **umask** of the process removes bits from the request before the file is made. It is a mask of what to take away, which is why it reads backwards from everything else.

The arithmetic is `requested & ~umask`. The usual defaults: programs ask for `0666` for a data file and `0777` for a directory or a program, and a umask of `0022` turns those into `0644` and `0755`. A umask of `0077` turns them into `0600` and `0700`, which is what you want for anything private.

This is the answer to a puzzle that comes up on every robot. Your service writes a log, another service in the same group cannot read it, and the mode is `0600` although the code asked for `0664`. Nobody changed it: the umask of the service removed the group bits. In a systemd unit you set `UMask=0002` and the problem is gone.

The umask can only take bits away. It cannot add one. A file created with a request of `0600` under a umask of `0000` is still `0600`, so if you want a file to be group readable, the program has to ask for it and the umask has to allow it. Both.

lessons.title: Root Is Not a Requirement
lessons.goal: Replace root with the two or three capabilities a robot service actually uses.
lessons.theory:
Root is not one permission, it is about forty. Linux splits them into **capabilities**, and a process can hold exactly the ones it needs and none of the rest. A service that runs as root because of one privileged operation is carrying thirty nine it will never use, and every one of them is available to any bug in it.

The ones that come up on a robot:

- `CAP_SYS_NICE`, to raise scheduling priority or pin to a core. This is what a control loop wants after lesson 5 of chapter 0.
- `CAP_NET_RAW`, to open raw sockets, which is what ping and most CAN tooling need.
- `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, to bind a port below 1024.
- `CAP_SYS_RAWIO`, to touch `/dev/mem` and raw ports.
- `CAP_SYS_TIME`, to set the system clock, which a GPS receiver service wants.

In a systemd unit you write `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_SYS_NICE` and `User=robot`, and the service starts unprivileged with that one extra power. On a plain binary, `setcap` writes the same thing into the file.

And notice what is not on the list. Reading a sensor, writing a GPIO, opening a serial port: none of those need a capability. They need the group from the last three lessons. Reach for a capability only when no group can give you the thing.

              "map /dev/mem": "CAP_SYS_RAWIO",
              "set the clock from gps": "CAP_SYS_TIME"}

            ("lidar driver", ["read the serial port"]),

lessons.title: The Directory You Cannot Enter
lessons.goal: Find the component of a path that blocks a user, which is almost never the file at the end.
lessons.theory:
On a directory the three bits mean something else. `r` lets you list the names inside it. `x` lets you **enter** it, which means resolving a name through it. `w` lets you create and delete entries in it, and notice that deleting a file is a write to the directory, not to the file.

`x` without `r` is a normal and useful combination: mode `0711` on a home directory lets anybody reach `/home/robot/public/thing` if they know the exact name, while nobody can list what is in there.

The important consequence for a robot is that opening `/opt/rover/etc/pins.yaml` needs `x` on `/`, on `/opt`, on `/opt/rover` and on `/opt/rover/etc`, and only then the read bit on the file. One directory in the middle with mode `0750` and a group your service is not in blocks everything below it, and the error you get is `EACCES` on the file at the end, which is the one place the problem is not.

So when a path fails, walk it from the root. `namei -l /opt/rover/etc/pins.yaml` prints the mode and owner of every component in one command and finds it immediately.

lessons.title: The Service That Drops What It Does Not Need
lessons.goal: Build the smallest privilege set a service can run with and still do its job.
lessons.theory:
Now put the last five lessons together, because this is the decision you make for every service on the robot.

Start from nothing: an ordinary user, no capabilities, no write access outside its own directory. Then add, one at a time, only what the service demonstrably needs.

- It opens `/dev/rover/lidar`: add the group that owns the node, `SupplementaryGroups=dialout`. No capability.
- It writes a log to `/var/log/rover`: give that directory to the group and set `UMask=0002`. No capability.
- It raises its own scheduling priority: `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_SYS_NICE`. Not root.
- It needs nothing else: `ProtectSystem=strict` makes the whole filesystem read only except what you list, `PrivateTmp=yes` gives it a temporary directory nobody else can see, `NoNewPrivileges=yes` stops any child from gaining more than the parent has.

The result reads like a description of the service, and it is the most useful documentation a robot has. A newcomer looking at a unit with `User=robot`, one group and one capability knows what that service can do to the machine. A unit with no `User=` tells them nothing, because the answer is everything.

Chapter 7 writes these lines into a real unit file. This lesson decides what goes in them.
lessons.task: Fill in `privileges` so it collects the groups a service needs from `NODE_GROUP` and the capabilities from `CAPABILITY`, and reports `root` only when something in the list genuinely has no other answer.
lessons.hint: One loop with three branches in the order of least power first, so root is only reached when the first two have refused.

lessons.title: The Bit That Protects a Shared Directory
lessons.goal: Use the sticky bit so two services can share a directory without deleting each other's files.
lessons.theory:
Two services both write into `/run/rover`. The directory has to be group writable or neither can create anything. But write on a directory means create **and delete**, so each service can remove the other's socket, and one day one of them does, during cleanup, at start up, and the other one has been dead for an hour before anybody notices.

The **sticky bit** is the fix, and `/tmp` is where you have already seen it. Mode `1777`, and `ls -l` shows the last character as `t` instead of `x`. In a directory with the sticky bit set, you may only delete or rename an entry if you own the entry, or you own the directory, or you are root. Everybody can still create their own files, which is the point.

For a robot that means `/run/rover` at mode `1770` with the group both services share. Each one owns what it writes, neither can touch the other's, and the whole directory is invisible to anybody outside the group. In a systemd unit, `RuntimeDirectory=rover` with `RuntimeDirectoryMode=1770` creates it at start and removes it at stop.

The bit only has this meaning on directories. On a regular file it is a leftover from an older Unix and today it does nothing.

lessons.title: The Audit Before First Power
lessons.goal: Sweep every node the robot will open and report the ones that are wrong in either direction.
lessons.theory:
Two failures live at opposite ends of the same scale and both belong in one report.

A node the robot **cannot** open stops the machine at start up, loudly, and gets fixed in ten minutes. A node that is **world writable** does not stop anything. Mode `0666` on a motor controller means any process on the board, including one that got in through a web port, can drive the wheels. Nothing will ever tell you, because everything works.

So the audit asks two questions of every node in the inventory. Can the service user get the access it needs? And can anybody who is not in the group get access it should not have? The first is `EACCES` waiting to happen, the second is the finding that matters and the one nobody looks for.

A third check is worth having: a node with a group nobody is a member of. That one passes the first question as long as the other bits are open, which means somebody made it world accessible instead of fixing the group, and it is the fingerprint of a `chmod 777` during a bad afternoon.

Run this on the image before it ships. It takes a page of code and it has caught real machines.

lessons.title: Four Programs Before Yours
lessons.goal: Follow the handover chain from the boot ROM to init and find the first stage that can do a given job.
lessons.theory:
Nothing on an embedded board goes straight to Linux. Four programs run first, each one bigger and more capable than the last, and each one exists because the one before it could not do the job.

- The **boot ROM** is burned into the chip and cannot be changed. It runs from internal SRAM because the DRAM controller is not configured yet, so it is tiny, and all it can do is read raw sectors from one medium and jump to what it finds.
- The **SPL**, the secondary program loader, fits in that same handful of kilobytes. Its one important job is initialising the DRAM, after which there is finally memory to load something big into.
- **U-Boot** is a real program in DRAM. It can read filesystems, talk to the network, print a prompt on the serial port, and it is the stage that loads the kernel, the device tree and, if there is one, the initramfs, then jumps into the kernel with the command line.
- The **kernel** brings up the drivers, mounts the root filesystem, and executes one program: `init`, as process 1.

Knowing which stage can do what is what makes boot problems solvable. A board that prints nothing at all died before U-Boot, so the serial console is your only witness. A board that prints U-Boot and then stops did not find a kernel. A board that prints kernel messages and then panics did not find a root filesystem. Three different searches, and the console tells you which one you are in.
