lessons.title: The Line the Kernel Was Given
lessons.goal: Parse the kernel command line into its settings and its bare flags.
lessons.theory:
The bootloader hands the kernel one string, and `/proc/cmdline` is that string, unchanged. It is the first thing to read when a board behaves differently from the one next to it, because a surprising amount of behaviour is decided here and nowhere else.

The syntax is space separated tokens of two shapes. A token with an equals sign is a setting, `root=PARTUUID=6c586e13-02`, and note that the value can contain its own equals sign, which is why you split once and not on every one. A token without is a flag that is true by being present: `quiet`, `rootwait`, `splash`.

The settings that matter on a robot:

- `console=serial0,115200` sends kernel messages to the serial port. Without it you get no output at all from a headless board and every boot problem becomes guesswork.
- `root=` says which filesystem to mount, and the next lesson is about how to write it.
- `rootwait` waits for that device to appear instead of panicking, which matters when the root is on something enumerated asynchronously.
- `quiet` hides most messages, which is how a product boots and the opposite of how you debug one.

A key can appear more than once. Two `console=` tokens mean the messages go to both, and the last one becomes `/dev/console` for user space. So a parser that keeps only the last value is throwing away half the answer.

lessons.title: The Root That Does Not Move
lessons.goal: Choose a root specification that survives somebody plugging in a second disk.
lessons.theory:
`root=/dev/mmcblk0p2` works until the day it does not. Add a USB stick to a board that boots from an SD card and the enumeration can shift; move the same image to a board with eMMC and `mmcblk0` is the internal storage while the card became `mmcblk1`. The kernel then panics with `Unable to mount root fs`, which is a very loud way of saying the name moved.

The kernel accepts three stable forms and one unstable one.

- `root=PARTUUID=6c586e13-02` names the partition by an identifier written in the partition table. This is the one Raspberry Pi images use and the one to prefer, because it survives being written to a different card.
- `root=UUID=...` names the filesystem itself by the identifier inside its superblock. Equally stable, and it follows the data if the partition is moved.
- `root=LABEL=rootfs` names it by a label you chose. Stable and readable, as long as you never have two.
- `root=/dev/mmcblk0p2` names a position in an enumeration order nobody promised you.

Two flags go with this. `rootwait` waits indefinitely for the device to appear, which is what you want when the root is behind USB or an SD card that takes a moment. `rootdelay=5` waits a fixed number of seconds instead, which is the older and worse version of the same idea.

lessons.title: A Filesystem in RAM First
lessons.goal: Decide whether this board needs an initramfs, instead of shipping one because everybody does.
lessons.theory:
An **initramfs** is a small filesystem the bootloader loads into RAM alongside the kernel. The kernel unpacks it, runs `/init` from it, and that script does whatever is needed to reach the real root, then hands over.

It exists for one reason: the kernel has to mount the root filesystem, and sometimes mounting it needs code the kernel does not have loaded yet. If the driver for your storage is a module, the module lives on the storage you cannot mount. If the root is encrypted, somebody has to ask for the key. If the root is on LVM, on RAID or over the network, all of that has to happen before there is a root.

A general purpose distribution ships one because it cannot know what your machine is. An embedded board can usually skip it: build the storage and filesystem drivers **into** the kernel rather than as modules, and the kernel mounts the root itself. That removes a stage, a file to keep in sync, and about a second of boot time.

So the question is not whether initramfs is good, it is whether anything has to happen before the root can be mounted. If the answer is no, do not ship one.

lessons.title: Init Is PID 1
lessons.goal: Write the init script of an initramfs: mount the kernel filesystems, find the real root, and hand over.
lessons.theory:
The kernel unpacks the initramfs and runs `/init` as **process 1**. Process 1 is special: it is never allowed to exit. If it does, the kernel panics with `Attempted to kill init`, which is the message you get when your script has a typo on the last line.

The script does four things, always in this order.

First it mounts the filesystems the rest of the work needs: `proc` on `/proc`, `sysfs` on `/sys`, `devtmpfs` on `/dev`. Nothing works before this, including reading the kernel command line, which lives in `/proc/cmdline`.

Then it finds the real root. That means reading `root=` out of `/proc/cmdline`, because hard coding it here defeats the point of having it on the command line at all.

Then it mounts that root somewhere, by convention `/newroot`, read only, so a filesystem check is still possible afterwards.

Last, it hands over with `exec switch_root /newroot /sbin/init`. `switch_root` moves the mount to `/`, deletes the contents of the initramfs to give the RAM back, and executes the real init **in the same process**, so the new program is still process 1. The `exec` is not decoration: without it your shell stays around as process 1 with the real init as its child, and shutdown does not work.
lessons.task: Complete the script: read the root device from `/proc/cmdline` into `rootdev`, mount it read only on `/newroot`, and hand over with `switch_root`.

mount -t sysfs none /sys
mount -t devtmpfs none /dev

mkdir -p /newroot

# TODO: read root= from /proc/cmdline into rootdev, mount it, hand over

echo "init: nothing to hand over to yet"
sleep 1

#!/bin/sh

mount -t sysfs none /sys
mount -t devtmpfs none /dev

mkdir -p /newroot

rootdev=$(sed -n 's/.*root=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p' /proc/cmdline)

mount -o ro "$rootdev" /newroot

exec switch_root /newroot /sbin/init

lessons.title: The Timestamps in dmesg
lessons.goal: Find where the boot really went by reading the gaps between kernel messages, not the messages.
lessons.theory:
Every line of `dmesg` starts with the seconds since the kernel started, in brackets, with six decimals. On a board that takes eleven seconds to boot, the interesting information is not in any single line, it is in the **distance** between two of them.

A gap of four seconds between two consecutive messages means the kernel spent four seconds inside whatever the first line announced. That is almost always one of three things: a driver waiting for hardware that is not answering, a probe with a built in timeout, or the root filesystem being waited for. Reading the messages one at a time will not show you this, because each individual line looks perfectly normal.

So the method is mechanical. Parse the stamp off every line, take the difference with the line before, sort by the difference, and read the top three. On a first look at any board this finds the answer in under a minute, and it works the same on a boot that takes ninety seconds.

`dmesg -T` prints wall clock times instead, which is what you want for something that happened yesterday and not for boot timing. For boot, keep the seconds.

lessons.title: A Budget for the First Second
lessons.goal: Turn a boot into a table of stages against a budget and name the one worth attacking.
lessons.theory:
A robot that has to be moving five seconds after power on needs a boot budget, and a budget is a table, not a feeling. Measure each stage once, write down what it cost, and compare against what you promised.

The measurements come from four places. `dmesg` gives you kernel time, the first stamp to the last. `systemd-analyze` gives you the split between firmware, loader, kernel and user space in one line. `systemd-analyze blame` sorts your services by how long each took to start. And the difference between power on and the first kernel message is the bootloader, which no tool on the running system can see, so you time it with a stopwatch or a scope on a GPIO.

Then attack the biggest one, not the easiest one. Almost every embedded boot has a single dominant stage, and it is usually one of: U-Boot counting down its autoboot delay, which is a one line fix, an initramfs you did not need, a USB probe with a timeout behind it, or the graphical target on a machine with no screen.

What you must not do is optimise a stage that costs 80 milliseconds while another one costs four seconds. The table stops that argument before it starts.

lessons.title: The Root That Cannot Be Written
lessons.goal: Make a robot survive having its power cut by deciding, per path, what may be written and where it goes.
lessons.theory:
A robot loses power without warning. Not gracefully, not with a shutdown: somebody hits the emergency stop, or the battery protection cuts out mid write. A read only root filesystem is what turns that from a corrupted image into an event nobody notices.

Mounting the root read only is one word in the command line, `ro`, and then everything that writes breaks. That is the useful part: it forces you to say, for every path, what it really is.

- **Volatile**, gone at reboot, belongs on a `tmpfs`: `/run`, `/tmp`, the working files of a service. Fast, in RAM, never corrupted because there is nothing on disk.
- **Persistent**, must survive: maps, calibration, logs you will actually read. These go on a separate partition mounted read write, with a journalled filesystem, and nothing else on it.
- **Neither**, a program writing where it should not: a package writing into `/usr`, a library caching into its own install directory. Those are bugs, and read only root is what finds them.

`/etc` is the interesting case. Most of it is static, but `machine-id`, `resolv.conf` and a few others are written at boot, and the usual answer is a symlink into `/run` or a small overlay. Getting this list right once is the difference between a robot you can unplug and one you have to nurse.

lessons.title: Two Slots and a Way Back
lessons.goal: Update a robot in the field without being able to visit it when the update is bad.
lessons.theory:
A robot in a field, on a roof or inside a machine cannot be recovered with an SD card reader. So the update scheme has to assume the new image is broken and still leave the machine reachable.

The answer is **two slots**. The storage holds two complete root filesystems, A and B. The robot is running A, the update is written into B while A keeps working, and only then does the bootloader get told to try B next. Writing never touches the filesystem you are running from, so an interrupted update loses nothing.

The rollback is a counter. The bootloader keeps three numbers per slot: which slot to try, how many attempts are left, and whether that slot has ever been declared good. On each boot it decrements the attempts of the slot it is about to try. If the attempts reach zero without success, it switches to the other slot, which is the one that was working an hour ago.

Declaring success is the part people get wrong. The new image marks itself good only after the robot has actually done its job: services up, sensors answering, one clean control loop. A slot that marks itself good in a start up script has no rollback at all, because a robot that boots and then does nothing counts as a success.

`RAUC`, `swupdate` and `mender` all implement this, and U-Boot has the counter built into its environment. The logic below is theirs, and it fits in fifteen lines.
lessons.task: Fill in `boot_once` so a slot with attempts left is tried and its counter decremented, and a slot that has run out hands over to the other one.

lessons.title: A Unit Is Three Sections
lessons.goal: Write the service unit that starts a robot driver as an unprivileged user at boot.
lessons.theory:
A service on a modern Linux is a text file in `/etc/systemd/system` called `something.service`, and it has three sections.

`[Unit]` is about the service as a thing in the system: what it is called in the logs, and how it relates to other units. `Description=` is the sentence `systemctl status` prints, so write a real one.

`[Service]` is about the process. `ExecStart=` is the command, and it must be an **absolute path**, because there is no shell here and no `PATH` to search. `Type=simple` says the program stays in the foreground and does not fork, which is what almost every program you write should do. `User=` and `SupplementaryGroups=` are the lesson of chapter 5 applied: run as `robot`, add the group that owns the node.

`[Install]` is what `systemctl enable` reads. `WantedBy=multi-user.target` means "start me when the system reaches the normal running state". Without an `[Install]` section, enabling does nothing and the service simply never starts at boot, which is a very common first hour.

Three commands go with it: `systemctl daemon-reload` after editing the file, `systemctl enable --now rover-lidar` to switch it on for this boot and every one after, and `systemctl status rover-lidar` to see what happened.

lessons.title: After Is Not Requires
lessons.goal: Separate ordering from requirement, and see which of the four combinations is the one you meant.
lessons.theory:
These two are confused more than anything else in systemd, and they are completely independent.

`After=` is **ordering only**. It says: if both of us are being started, do not start me until it has finished starting. It says nothing about whether the other unit is started at all, and nothing about what happens if it fails.

`Requires=` is **requirement only**. It says: if I am started, start that too, and if it fails or is stopped, stop me. It says nothing about order, so without an `After=` systemd starts both at the same instant and your service races the thing it depends on. That race is the classic bug: it works on your desk and fails on the robot, because the timing is different.

So the four combinations, and only one of them is usually right:

- Neither: independent. Fine when they really are.
- `After=` alone: I run after it if it runs at all. Correct for something optional, like a network that may not exist.
- `Requires=` alone: pull it in, and race it. Almost always a mistake.
- Both: pull it in, wait for it, and die with it. This is what people mean when they write one of them.

`Wants=` is the softer `Requires=`: pull it in, but do not fail if it fails. For a robot, `Wants=` plus `After=` is the right shape for anything the machine should try to have and can survive without.

lessons.title: The Order Nobody Wrote Down
lessons.goal: Turn a pile of After= lines into the start up order they add up to, and refuse a set that eats itself.
lessons.theory:
No unit knows the whole order. Each one names the two or three things it must follow, and systemd works the rest out. What it is doing is a **topological sort**: repeatedly start everything whose dependencies are already up, until nothing is left.

Doing it yourself once is worth an afternoon of reading, because it makes two things obvious.

The first is that units with no relationship start **at the same time**, on purpose. That parallelism is where systemd gets its speed, and it is also why an ordering you forgot to declare works nine boots out of ten.

The second is what happens with a cycle. If A must follow B and B must follow A, no order exists. systemd deals with it by breaking the loop at an arbitrary point and logging `Found ordering cycle`, then dropping one of the units. The robot comes up with a service missing and nothing obviously wrong, which is the worst kind of failure. Your own sort should refuse instead, loudly, because you can afford to.

`systemd-analyze critical-chain rover.target` prints the real chain with the time each step took, and it is the tool that turns this from theory into a boot that is two seconds shorter.

lessons.title: When It Dies, Bring It Back
lessons.goal: Restart a crashed driver automatically, and stop restarting it when it is clearly never going to work.
lessons.theory:
A robot driver that dies at three in the morning should come back by itself. `Restart=on-failure` does that: systemd notices the process exited with a non zero status or a signal, waits `RestartSec=`, and starts it again.

`Restart=always` restarts even on a clean exit, which is right for something that is supposed to run forever and wrong for anything that legitimately finishes. `Restart=on-watchdog` is the one that pairs with the next lesson.

But a service that restarts forever is worse than one that stays down, because it looks alive. If the serial adapter is unplugged, the driver fails in 30 milliseconds, restarts, fails again, and you get thirty starts a second filling the journal and the processor.

That is what the rate limit is for, and it lives in `[Unit]`, not in `[Service]`, which is the detail everybody gets wrong the first time. `StartLimitIntervalSec=60` and `StartLimitBurst=4` mean: more than four starts inside any sixty second window and systemd gives up, puts the unit in `failed`, and stops trying. Then `systemctl status` says so and a supervisor can escalate.

Pick `RestartSec=` with the failure in mind. Two seconds is long enough that a hardware fault does not become a spin, and short enough that a transient hiccup costs nothing.

lessons.title: The Rate Limit That Gives Up
lessons.goal: Run the start limit yourself and see exactly which restart is the one that stops the machine trying.
lessons.theory:
The rule is a sliding window and nothing more. Keep the times of the recent starts, throw away everything older than `StartLimitIntervalSec`, and if what is left is more than `StartLimitBurst`, refuse.

Doing it by hand answers the question people argue about: is a service that crashes every thirty seconds going to be given up on? With a window of sixty and a burst of four, no, because only two starts are ever inside the window. And a service that crashes instantly, restarting every two seconds, hits five starts inside the window on the fifth one and is dropped. Two failures that feel similar and end completely differently.

The important part is what you do with that. A unit in `failed` state is a fact your supervisor can read: `systemctl is-failed rover-lidar` is a shell command with an exit status, and `OnFailure=rover-alert.service` starts another unit when it happens. That is how a robot tells somebody instead of quietly limping.

The opposite mistake is `StartLimitIntervalSec=0`, which disables the limit entirely. It exists for a reason and it is not a default you should copy from a forum: it turns every unfixable fault into an infinite loop.

lessons.title: Telling systemd You Are Alive
lessons.goal: Make a service report that it is ready and keep proving it, so a hung loop is noticed instead of tolerated.
lessons.theory:
A process that is running is not the same as a service that is working. A control loop deadlocked on a mutex is still a live process, still `active (running)` in `systemctl status`, and completely useless. `Type=simple` cannot tell the difference, because all it knows is that the process exists.

`Type=notify` fixes both halves. The program calls `sd_notify(0, "READY=1")` when it has finished starting, and systemd holds everything ordered after it until that message arrives. That removes the race where a dependent service starts against a driver that is up but not ready.

Then `WatchdogSec=5` turns the same channel into a heartbeat. systemd expects `WATCHDOG=1` at least every five seconds, and the convention is to send it at half the interval so a small delay is not fatal. Miss it and systemd treats the service as failed and acts on `Restart=on-watchdog`, which restarts precisely the case a plain restart policy cannot see: alive and stuck.

Two details matter. The heartbeat must be sent from the loop that can actually hang, not from a helper thread that keeps ticking while the real work is blocked, or you have built a watchdog that watches itself. And `NotifyAccess=main` says only the main process may send these messages, which stops a child from keeping a dead parent alive.

lessons.title: The Log Has Fields, Not Lines
lessons.goal: Query the journal the way it is actually stored, by field, instead of grepping text.
lessons.theory:
`journalctl` looks like a file of lines and is not. Every entry is a set of **fields**, and the human readable line is one field among many. That is why `journalctl -u rover-lidar -p err --since "10 min ago"` is exact where a `grep` over a text log is a guess.

The fields you will use: `MESSAGE` is the text. `PRIORITY` is a number from 0, emergency, to 7, debug, where 3 is an error and 6 is plain information. `_SYSTEMD_UNIT` is the unit that produced it, and the leading underscore means the journal filled it in, not the program, so it cannot be faked by a service claiming to be another. `_PID` and `_UID` are trusted the same way.

`journalctl -o json` gives you one JSON object per line, which is what you parse when you want a report rather than a read. A robot that mails you a summary of its night is fifteen lines on top of that.

Two settings decide whether any of this survives. By default the journal on many images is in `/run`, so it is gone at reboot, which is exactly when you want it. `Storage=persistent` in `journald.conf` puts it in `/var/log/journal`, and `SystemMaxUse=200M` stops it eating the card. On a read only root, that directory has to be on the writable partition from chapter 6.

lessons.title: The Service That Waits for the Device
lessons.goal: Bind a driver to the device it drives, so it starts when the hardware appears and stops when it is unplugged.
lessons.theory:
This closes the race from chapter 2. Every device udev knows about is also a **device unit**: `/dev/rover/lidar` is `dev-rover-lidar.device`, with the slashes turned into dashes. The unit becomes active when udev has finished processing the device, not when the node appears, so waiting for it waits for the permissions and the symlink too.

Two lines do the work. `After=dev-rover-lidar.device` is the ordering, so your service starts once the device is fully set up. `BindsTo=dev-rover-lidar.device` is the requirement, and it is stronger than `Requires=` in exactly the way you want here: if the device goes away, the service is stopped. Unplug the lidar and the driver stops cleanly instead of spinning on a descriptor that will never answer again. Plug it back in and, with a `WantedBy` on the device from a udev rule, it starts again.

The udev half is the line from chapter 4: `TAG+="systemd", ENV{SYSTEMD_WANTS}="rover-lidar.service"`. Without the `systemd` tag the device unit is not even tracked.

Two commands to keep: `systemctl list-units --type=device` shows what systemd currently believes is plugged in, and `systemd-escape --path /dev/rover/lidar` builds the unit name so you do not have to guess how a dash inside a name is escaped.
lessons.task: Bind the driver to its device: add `After=dev-rover-lidar.device` and `BindsTo=dev-rover-lidar.device` to `[Unit]`.

User=robot
SupplementaryGroups=dialout
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

lessons.title: Everything It Does Not Need
lessons.goal: Generate the hardening lines for a service from what it genuinely touches.
lessons.theory:
systemd can take things away from a service, and each one costs a line. The four that pay for themselves on a robot:

- `ProtectSystem=strict` mounts the whole filesystem read only for this service, and then `ReadWritePaths=` lists the exceptions. A service that only writes its own log directory gets exactly that and nothing else. This is chapter 6 enforced per service instead of per boot.
- `PrivateTmp=yes` gives the service its own `/tmp` that nobody else can see, which removes a whole family of attacks and also stops two services fighting over the same temporary file name.
- `NoNewPrivileges=yes` means nothing this service starts can gain more than it has, so a setuid binary it executes stays unprivileged.
- `DeviceAllow=` restricts which device nodes it may open at all, and with `PrivateDevices=yes` it gets a `/dev` containing almost nothing.

The reason to generate these from a list rather than copy them is that the list is the thing you actually maintain. When somebody adds a directory the service writes to, they add it to one place, and the unit follows. When they cannot say what it writes to, that is the finding.

`systemd-analyze security rover-lidar.service` scores a unit out of ten and names what is missing. It is worth running once on every service you own, and it is unkind in a useful way.

lessons.title: The Machine That Builds Is Not the Machine That Runs
lessons.goal: Name the kind of build you are doing from the three machines involved in it.
lessons.theory:
Three machines take part in a build, and they have names that are worth learning once because every toolchain error message uses them.

The **build** machine is the one running the compiler. The **host** machine is the one the program you are producing will run on. The **target** machine only matters when the thing you are producing is itself a compiler, and it is the machine that compiler will produce code for.

From those three, four situations:

- Build and host are the same: an ordinary **native** build. Your laptop compiling a program for your laptop.
- Build and host differ: a **cross** build. Your laptop compiling the robot program for an ARM board, which is what this chapter is about.
- Target differs from host: you are **building a compiler**, one that runs on the host and produces code for the target.
- All three differ: a **Canadian cross**, building on machine one a compiler that runs on machine two and produces code for machine three. You will meet it exactly once, when somebody hands you a toolchain built that way and something is subtly wrong with it.

Autotools spells these out as `--build`, `--host` and `--target`, and getting `--host` wrong is the single most common way a cross build silently produces native binaries that will not run on the board.

lessons.title: A Name With Four Fields
lessons.goal: Read a toolchain prefix and say what machine it produces code for.
lessons.theory:
`aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` is not a name somebody invented, it is four fields with dashes between them and a trailing dash before the tool.

The fields are **architecture**, **vendor**, **operating system** and **ABI**. The vendor is usually dropped because nobody cares, which is why most prefixes you see have three fields rather than four:

- `aarch64-linux-gnu`: 64 bit ARM, Linux, the GNU C library. A Raspberry Pi 4 on a 64 bit image.
- `arm-linux-gnueabihf`: 32 bit ARM, Linux, GNU with the hard float ABI. A 32 bit Pi image, and the next lesson is about that `hf`.
- `x86_64-pc-linux-gnu`: all four fields, and `pc` is the vendor placeholder.
- `arm-none-eabi`: the operating system field is `none`, which means bare metal. No kernel, no C library that talks to one. This is the prefix a microcontroller build uses, and it is the one the RTOS course lives in.

Reading the prefix tells you before you compile anything whether the binary will run. A program built with `arm-none-eabi` will never run on a Linux board, and one built with `arm-linux-gnueabihf` will never run on a board whose libraries are `gnueabi` without the `hf`.
lessons.task: Fill in `parse_triplet` so a four field name is split as it stands and a three field name gets `unknown` in the vendor position that was left out.
lessons.hint: Two branches on the length of parts, and the three field case is the one where the second field is not the vendor.

lessons.title: What the Binary Confesses
lessons.goal: Read the ELF header of a compiled file and say which machine it is really for.
lessons.theory:
Every executable and every shared library on Linux starts with an **ELF header**, and the first 24 bytes of it answer the question you care about after a cross build: is this actually for the board.

The first four bytes are the magic, `\x7fELF`. Byte 4 is the class, 1 for 32 bit and 2 for 64 bit. Byte 5 is the endianness, 1 for little endian. Bytes 6 to 15 are the version and padding.

Then two 16 bit numbers and a 32 bit one: the type, where 2 is a plain executable and 3 is the position independent kind that modern toolchains produce by default, and the **machine**, which is the field that decides everything. 40 is ARM, 183 is AArch64, 62 is x86-64, 243 is RISC-V.

`file rover` prints all of this in a sentence and `readelf -h rover` prints it as a table, and you should run one of them on every binary you copy to a board. The failure it prevents is the confusing one: you cross compiled, something in the build fell back to the host compiler, and the board answers `cannot execute binary file: Exec format error`, which people spend hours reading as a permissions problem.
lessons.task: Fill in `describe` so it refuses anything without the magic, and otherwise reports the class and the machine from `CLASSES` and `MACHINES`.
lessons.hint: The magic is a slice of the first four bytes, the class is a single byte you index, and the two numbers after the identifier are unpacked together.

lessons.title: Hard Float Is Not a Suggestion
lessons.goal: Catch an ABI mismatch between a program and a library before the linker does it with a worse message.
lessons.theory:
Two binaries for the same architecture can still be unable to speak to each other, because the **ABI** decides how arguments are passed and they have to agree.

On 32 bit ARM the split that bites is floating point. In the **soft float** ABI, `float` and `double` arguments travel in integer registers, and the code works on a chip with no floating point unit. In the **hard float** ABI, they travel in the VFP registers, which is faster and requires the unit to exist. Same instructions, same processor, incompatible calling conventions.

ELF records which one in the flags field of the header: `0x400` is hard float, `0x200` is soft float, and zero means the object did not say. The linker reads it, and when a program built one way meets a library built the other, it refuses with a sentence people have stared at for years: `uses VFP register arguments, output does not`.

The `hf` at the end of `arm-linux-gnueabihf` is exactly this flag, and it is why a Raspberry Pi 32 bit image needs the `hf` toolchain and a plain `arm-linux-gnueabi` one produces libraries the system will not link against.

On 64 bit ARM the question does not arise: AArch64 has one floating point ABI and it is mandatory.
lessons.task: Fill in `float_abi` so it reads the flags with `HARD_FLOAT` and `SOFT_FLOAT`, and `compatible` so two objects only link when neither of them contradicts the other.

lessons.title: The Root That Is Not Yours
lessons.goal: Point every include and library path at the sysroot, and find the flag that is still reaching into your laptop.
lessons.theory:
A cross compiler needs headers and libraries for the **board**, not for the machine it is running on. That collection is the **sysroot**: a directory that looks like the root filesystem of the target, with `usr/include` and `usr/lib` inside it, usually copied from the board or unpacked from the image.

`--sysroot=/opt/rover/sysroot` tells the compiler to look there, and from then on `-I/usr/include` means the one inside the sysroot. That is the whole idea, and it works until somebody adds an absolute path by hand.

That is the failure worth being able to see. A `-I/usr/include/eigen3` written into a Makefile by a developer on their laptop reaches into the **build** machine, so the compile succeeds with x86 headers describing structure sizes that are wrong for ARM. Nothing fails at build time. The program runs on the board and produces nonsense, or crashes somewhere unrelated, and the cause is a header from a different architecture.

The check is mechanical: any absolute path in a flag that is not inside the sysroot is a leak. Run it over your flags before you trust a build, and put `pkg-config` in the same frame of mind, because `PKG_CONFIG_SYSROOT_DIR` exists for exactly this reason and nothing sets it for you.

lessons.title: CROSS_COMPILE Is Just a Prefix
lessons.goal: Turn a native Makefile into one that builds for the board by changing the tools, not the rules.
lessons.theory:
Almost every embedded Makefile, including the kernel's own, uses one variable for this. `CROSS_COMPILE` holds the prefix, trailing dash included, and every tool is that prefix followed by its name: `$(CROSS_COMPILE)gcc`, `$(CROSS_COMPILE)ld`, `$(CROSS_COMPILE)objcopy`, `$(CROSS_COMPILE)strip`.

Written that way, one variable on the command line switches the whole build: `make CROSS_COMPILE=aarch64-linux-gnu-`. Leave it empty and the same Makefile builds natively, which is what you want for running the unit tests on your laptop.

Use `?=` rather than `=` for it. `?=` assigns only if the variable has no value yet, so the environment and the command line still win, and the file carries a sensible default instead of a decision.

The other half is the sysroot, and it has to reach both the compiler and the linker: the compiler needs the headers, the linker needs the libraries, and `--sysroot` in `CFLAGS` alone gives you a build that compiles and then fails at link time with symbols that clearly exist.

`CC := $(CROSS_COMPILE)gcc` uses the immediate form on purpose. With a plain `=` the variable is expanded every time it is used, which for a compiler name is both slower and harder to reason about.
lessons.task: Point the build at the board: make `CC` the prefixed compiler and add `--sysroot=$(SYSROOT)` to both `CFLAGS` and `LDFLAGS`.

OBJECTS := main.o motion.o

	$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -o $@ $(OBJECTS)

%.o: %.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c -o $@ $<

clean:
	rm -f rover $(OBJECTS)

lessons.title: Teaching CMake Where the Robot Lives
lessons.goal: Write the toolchain file that makes CMake build for the board, and stop it finding your laptop's libraries.
lessons.theory:
CMake does not take a `CROSS_COMPILE` variable. It takes a **toolchain file**, passed once at configure time with `cmake -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=aarch64.cmake ..`, and read before anything else so the compiler tests run against the right compiler.

The first two lines say what the machine is. `CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME` set to anything at all is what tells CMake this is a cross build, and setting it to `Linux` is what makes the whole thing behave. `CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR` is documentation for your own project.

Then the compilers, by their prefixed names, and `CMAKE_SYSROOT` for the headers and libraries.

The last three lines are the ones everybody forgets, and they are the whole point of the file. `find_package` and `find_library` search the machine they are running on, which is your laptop, and will happily hand the build an x86 library. `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH` says where to search instead, and three mode variables say what to do per kind. `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM` is set to `NEVER`, because tools that run during the build have to be native. `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY` and `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE` are set to `ONLY`, because those must come from the board and nowhere else.

Without those three, a cross build finds native libraries, links them, and the error arrives on the board.

lessons.title: Static Costs Space, Dynamic Costs Trust
lessons.goal: Choose between linking statically and dynamically for each program on the robot, with a reason you can defend.
lessons.theory:
Linking statically copies the library into your binary. Linking dynamically leaves a reference that `ld.so` resolves at start up from the shared object on the board.

Static is tempting on a robot. One file to copy, no dependency to install, nothing that can be upgraded underneath you, and a start up that skips the dynamic loader entirely. For a small tool that has to work on an image you do not control, it is the right answer.

It has two hard limits, and both are refusals rather than trade offs. A statically linked glibc cannot use `dlopen`, so any program that loads a plugin at run time is out. And name resolution, `getaddrinfo` and friends, loads its backends through the same mechanism, so a static program that resolves a hostname either fails or silently behaves differently from every other program on the machine. glibc warns about this at link time and everybody ignores it.

Dynamic has one cost that matters here: the library has to be on the board, at a version whose ABI matches. If it is not, the program does not start, and the message names a symbol version rather than a package.

So the decision is short. If it needs `dlopen` or name resolution, dynamic, no argument. Otherwise, if the library is already on the image, dynamic. If it is not, static and copy one file.

lessons.title: Smaller Than It Was
lessons.goal: Work out what a binary actually occupies on the board, which is a small fraction of the file you built.
lessons.theory:
A freshly built binary with debug information can be four megabytes while the code inside it is a hundred and fifty kilobytes. On a board with a small flash that difference decides whether the image fits, and it is worth being able to compute rather than guess.

Sections split into three kinds.

**Loaded from flash**: `.text`, the code, and `.rodata`, the constants, and `.data`, the initialised variables. These take space both in the file and in memory.

**Allocated but not stored**: `.bss`, the variables that start at zero. It occupies RAM at run time and nothing in the file, because there is nothing to store: the loader just zeroes it.

**Neither**: `.symtab`, `.strtab` and everything starting with `.debug`. These are for the debugger, and on most binaries they are the overwhelming majority of the file. `strip` removes them, `objcopy --only-keep-debug` saves them somewhere else first, and `arm-linux-gnueabihf-strip` is the cross version, which matters because the native `strip` will refuse a foreign binary.

`size rover` prints the first two groups and `readelf -S rover` prints every section with its size. The habit worth having: keep the unstripped binary next to the stripped one, because a core dump from the board is unreadable without it.

lessons.title: The Inventory of a Board
lessons.goal: Walk sysfs and produce the list of every device this board actually has.
lessons.theory:
The project of this chapter is a commissioning pass: a program you run once on a new board, or on every boot of a robot you care about, that answers whether the machine is what you think it is. It starts with an inventory, because every check after this one is a comparison against a list.

`/sys/class` is the right place to walk. It has one directory per subsystem, `gpio`, `pwm`, `tty`, `i2c-dev`, `thermal`, `net`, and inside each one a directory or a symlink per device. Two levels of `os.listdir` and you have the whole machine, without parsing anything.

Two habits make the result usable. Sort at every level, so two runs of the program produce the same list and a difference between two boards is a difference and not an ordering. And record the subsystem next to the name, because `i2c-1` and `ttyUSB1` mean nothing on their own and a great deal next to the class they belong to.

The inventory is also the thing you keep. Store it after the first successful commissioning, compare on every boot afterwards, and a device that stopped appearing becomes a line in a report instead of a robot that behaves strangely.

        handle = open(full, "w")

lessons.title: The Names the Robot Will Use
lessons.goal: Run your own rules over the inventory and produce the name every device will answer to.
lessons.theory:
Now apply chapter 4 to the inventory. Each rule is a subsystem, a set of attributes that must all match, and the link name to give whatever matches. Running them yourself, before the board is in the robot, answers two questions that udev will not answer for you.

The first is whether every device you depend on gets a name. A rule that matches nothing is silent on the board: the robot simply opens a path that does not exist, gets `ENOENT`, and reports a hardware fault that is really a typo in a serial number.

The second is the opposite, and it is the one worth building the tool for: which devices got **no** rule. Those keep their enumeration name, which means they work today and move tomorrow. On a commissioning report, an unmatched device is not an error, it is a decision somebody has to make: either it does not matter, or a rule is missing.

Matching all the attributes of one rule against one device is the same predicate as chapter 4, and it stays exactly as strict: every attribute in the rule has to be present with the right value, and a device that lacks one of them does not match at all.

lessons.title: The Order It Comes Up In
lessons.goal: Build the start up order for the robot and hold back the services whose hardware is not on this board.
lessons.theory:
Chapter 7 sorted units by their dependencies. On a real machine there is a second question that has to be asked at the same time: is the device this unit is bound to actually here.

A unit with `BindsTo=` a device that does not exist will never start, and systemd is right not to start it. What is unhelpful is what it looks like from outside: the robot comes up, four services out of five are running, and the fifth is `inactive (dead)` with no error anywhere, because nothing failed. Nobody notices until the arm does not move.

So the commissioning pass does both at once. Take the units, take the inventory from the previous lessons, and split them: the ones that can start, in a valid order, and the ones held back with the device that is missing named next to them. A held back unit is not necessarily a fault, a robot without an arm fitted is a legitimate configuration, but it has to appear on the report as a decision rather than as silence.

The ordering itself is the sort from chapter 7, with one addition: a unit that depends on a held back unit is held back too, because its dependency will never be satisfied.
lessons.task: Fill in `commission` so a unit whose device is missing is held back, a unit that waits for a held unit is held too and says which one it waits for, and the rest come out in dependency order.
lessons.hint: Three lines after blocked is computed: only act when the list is not empty, record the first name in it, and stop considering this unit on this pass.

lessons.title: The Pins, Claimed and Released
lessons.goal: Turn a pin configuration into the exact sequence of sysfs writes, refusing a plan that claims a line twice.
lessons.theory:
This is chapter 1 turned into something you can put in a file. A robot has a table of pins: which line, what it is for, whether it is an input or an output, and what the PWM channels should be set to. The bring up program reads that table and produces writes.

Two things have to happen before any write. The plan is checked for a line claimed twice, because two subsystems fighting over one pin is the chapter 3 conflict arriving at run time, and the second claim fails with `EBUSY` halfway through a bring up, leaving the robot half configured. And the order within each device is fixed: for GPIO, export then direction, and prefer the atomic `low` or `high` over `out` followed by a write. For PWM, export, period, duty cycle, then enable.

The other half is the release list, and it is built at the same time as the plan, not afterwards. Every claim you make goes into a list that a `finally` walks in reverse. Built that way, a bring up that fails in the middle unwinds exactly what it managed to do, and the next run starts clean instead of meeting the `EBUSY` from chapter 1.

Reverse order matters for the same reason it does anywhere else: what you claimed last may depend on what you claimed first.
lessons.task: Fill in `plan` so a repeated line is reported instead of planned, every claim is written down in `releases`, and the writes come out in the order the drivers accept.

CONFIG = [("estop", "gpio", 17, "in"),
          ("beacon", "gpio", 27, "low"),
          ("steer", "pwm", 0, (20000000, 1500000)),
          ("drive", "pwm", 1, (20000000, 1200000)),
          ("spare", "gpio", 27, "in")]


def plan(config):
    writes = []
    releases = []
    conflicts = []
    claimed = set()
    for name, kind, line, setting in config:
        if (kind, line) in claimed:
            conflicts.append("%s wants %s line %d, already claimed" % (name, kind, line))
            continue
        claimed.add((kind, line))
        if kind == "gpio":
            releases.append("/sys/class/gpio/unexport <- %d" % line)
            writes.append(("/sys/class/gpio/export", line))
            writes.append(("/sys/class/gpio/gpio%d/direction" % line, setting))
        else:
            period, duty = setting
            releases.append("/sys/class/pwm/pwmchip0/unexport <- %d" % line)
            writes.append(("/sys/class/pwm/pwmchip0/export", line))
            writes.append(("/sys/class/pwm/pwmchip0/pwm%d/period" % line, period))
            writes.append(("/sys/class/pwm/pwmchip0/pwm%d/duty_cycle" % line, duty))
            writes.append(("/sys/class/pwm/pwmchip0/pwm%d/enable" % line, 1))
    return (writes, releases, conflicts)


writes, releases, conflicts = plan(CONFIG)
print("writes:")
for path, value in writes:
    print("  ", path.ljust(28), "<-", value)
print("release order:", list(reversed(releases)))
print("conflicts:", conflicts)
lessons.hint: One branch per kind. The release is appended before the writes, so a failure on the very first write still has something to undo.

lessons.title: The Permissions Audit Before First Power
lessons.goal: Check every node the robot will open against the user it will run as, before the robot runs as that user.
lessons.theory:
Chapter 5 built the pieces. This is where they are run against a real list, and the value of doing it here is that every failure it finds is a failure that would otherwise happen at three in the morning with the machine on a table you cannot reach.

For every node in the plan, three inputs: the group that owns it, the mode, and what the service needs to do with it. Against one more: the groups the service user is in. That is enough to answer the question exactly, using the check from lesson 3 of chapter 5.

The report has three outcomes and they need different reactions. **Unreachable** means the robot will not start: fix the udev rule or the group membership. **World writable** means the robot will start and anything else on the board can drive it: fix the mode. **Reachable through the other bits** is the quiet one, a node the service can only open because it is open to everybody, and it passes the naive check while being the same finding as world writable.

That third case is why the audit reports **how** access was obtained and not just whether it was. A pass that does not say which of the three bit groups answered is a pass you cannot act on.
lessons.task: Fill in `how` so it names which set of bits granted the access, `group` when the user is in the owning group, `other` when it is only the last digit, and `none` when there is no access at all.

lessons.title: The First Second, Measured
lessons.goal: Cut a real boot log into named stages and say which stage owns the time.
lessons.theory:
The budget from chapter 6 was a table somebody typed. This is the same table built from the log the machine produced, which is the only version that stays true.

The method is markers. Choose a handful of lines that mean a stage finished, find each of them in the log, and the time of a stage is the distance from the previous marker to this one. Four markers cover almost every board: the first kernel message, the root filesystem being mounted, the basic system target being reached, and your own service announcing that the robot is ready. That last one has to be printed by your program, and printing it is the cheapest instrumentation you will ever add.

Then compare against the budget and name the biggest stage. Not the biggest total, the biggest **stage**, because that is the only number anybody can act on.

Two cautions. A marker that appears twice takes its first occurrence, so choose lines that are unique or take the first deliberately. And a marker that never appears at all means the boot did not reach that stage, which is a finding in itself and must not silently become a zero.
lessons.task: Fill in `stages` so each marker becomes a stage with the time since the previous one, and a marker that never appears is recorded as `never reached, the boot did not get this far` instead of a number.
lessons.starter:
LOG = ["[    0.000000] Booting Linux on physical CPU 0x0",
       "[    0.884210] Machine model: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B",
       "[    2.114903] EXT4-fs (mmcblk0p2): mounted filesystem",
       "[    3.020117] systemd[1]: Reached target Basic System",
       "[    5.775401] rover-mission[412]: robot ready"]

MARKERS = [("kernel start", "Booting Linux"),
           ("root mounted", "EXT4-fs (mmcblk0p2): mounted"),
           ("basic system", "Reached target Basic System"),
           ("robot ready", "robot ready"),
           ("arm homed", "arm homed")]

BUDGET = 5.0


def stamp(line):
    return float(line[1:line.index("]")])


def find(needle):
    for line in LOG:
        if needle in line:
            return stamp(line)
    return None


def stages():
    out = []
    previous = 0.0
    for label, needle in MARKERS:
        at = find(needle) or previous
        # TODO: a marker that never appeared is a finding, not a zero
        out.append((label, at - previous))
        previous = at
    return out


measured = stages()
for label, took in measured:
    print(label.ljust(14), "%6.3f s" % took if isinstance(took, float) else took)
real = [(label, took) for label, took in measured if isinstance(took, float)]
print("total: %.3f s against a budget of %.1f s" % (sum(t for _, t in real), BUDGET))
print("biggest stage:", max(real, key=lambda row: row[1])[0])

lessons.title: The Commissioning Report
lessons.goal: Put the whole chapter into one verdict, and make the fixes change it.
lessons.theory:
The last thing. Six checks have run, each one producing findings, and now somebody has to decide whether this machine goes into a robot. That decision needs a report with exactly three properties.

It has to be **short**: one line per check, a verdict, and the count of findings. A report nobody reads has failed at the only thing it does.

It has to distinguish **blocking** from **noted**. An unreachable node blocks: the robot will not work. A device with no udev rule is noted: it works today and somebody has to decide. Mixing the two produces a report that is always red, which is the same as a report that is always green.

And it has to be **re run after the fixes**, in the same session, so the change is visible. That is the difference between a report and a complaint. Below, the first pass fails on two blocking findings, the fixes are applied, and the second pass is the one you keep.

The commands behind each line are the ones from this course: `udevadm info` for the names, `ls -l` for the modes, `systemd-analyze` for the boot, `systemctl list-dependencies` for the order. What you built here is the thing that runs them all at once and gives one answer.
lessons.task: Fill in `verdict` so it answers `BLOCKING` for a check with blocking findings, `NOTED` for one with only noted findings and `PASS` for a clean one, and read the second pass against the first.
